Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Connaught Place ahead of today's protest. We are tracing the suspension order.

New Delhi, 2 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services in and around Connaught Place, New Delhi, this morning. At 9:40 am, Jio subscribers in the area received a message stating: "As per government instructions Internet services have been stopped in your area till further notice." The shutdown took effect before a protest called for 11 am at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner, had even begun. 

Delhi Police has refused permission for the gathering, prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force across New Delhi district, and entry and exit at eleven metro stations have been closed. On Gandhi Jayanti, the answer to a call for protest in the capital has been to switch off the internet for everyone who lives, works, trades and reports in its centre. We call for the immediate restoration of services. 

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public does not know who directed this shutdown, on what grounds, over what area, or until when. IFF is attempting to trace the order and will make it public as soon as we obtain a copy.

In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Supreme Court held that speech and trade over the internet are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution, and that every suspension order must be published, reasoned, proportionate and limited in time. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, only the Union or State Home Secretary may issue such an order, for reasons recorded in writing. The order must be published and must specify the area, the services and a fixed duration and it may be passed only where no other reasonable means would serve. A shutdown announced to subscribers as lasting "till further notice", imposed before a single person had assembled, cannot be squared with these safeguards. It follows repeated suspensions around Jantar Mantar in July 2026. Switching off the network is becoming a routine response to protest in the national capital. IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. 

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore mobile internet services in Connaught Place and all affected parts of Central Delhi.

2. Publish the suspension order forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.

3. Disclose the issuing authority, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation.

4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and make its findings public.

Statement: Instagram censors a cartoon about censorship. IFF will challenge it.
A cartoon on comedy, copyright and the IT Rules has been withheld in India by an automated system that cites no order and gives no reasons.

On 27 October 2026, Instagram withheld in India a cartoon by Aadvik (@aaaaadvik ) who first published on 29 September 2026 as a collaborative post on the accounts of IFF, Aadvik and stand-up comedian Pulkit Mani. It shows a panicked man at a console in the image and style of the Prime Minister with red buttons marked "Censor", "Copyright" and "IT Rules", while a comic performs on a screen above him. Its caption reads, "Quick, check if comedy counts as a violation of copyright or a matter of national security." The post asked who decides what gets taken down, and on what grounds.

Instagram has now answered this literally by taking it down after close to a month. Its notice says access was restricted "through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements" under the IT Rules, 2021. It names no order, authority, provision or ground. There was no prior notice and no chance to respond. The same cartoon remains available on IFF's X account. The post also carried an update on Pulkit Mani v. Meta Platforms Inc. & Ors., his Delhi High Court suit over fraudulent copyright strikes on his Instagram page, in which IFF appears for him pro bono. Meta, a defendant in that suit, has now hidden a post about it from Indian users in which it is the principal defendant.

In 1945, George Orwell wrote a preface to Animal Farm, a book four publishers had turned down. He noted, "the sinister fact about literary censorship in England," he observed, "is that it is largely voluntary." Unpopular ideas, he argued, could be silenced without any official ban, by institutions that guess what power wants and act first. The preface itself stayed unpublished until 1972 and in Nineteen Eighty-Four he gave this habit a machine, namely, the memory hole, a slot at the Ministry of Truth into which inconvenient records vanished, unexplained and beyond appeal. Today, the Ministry of Electronics and IT acts as this Ministry of Truth that covers up its gross incompetence in securing our cyber security by building an architecture of digital censorship that is implemented by technology platforms. It is under these IT Rules, 2021 that Instagram's "automated system" exists as a memory hole. It has swallowed a cartoon whose whole joke is a man reaching for the censor button without asking what comedy is. The absurdity Aadvik drew has now been actually demonstrated in stark reality.

This machine did not build itself and in April 2026, The Hindu reported that Meta automatically restricts content flagged by government and police in India, and wants a fresh government direction before restoring anything later found lawful. MeitY's unpublished advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026 pressed platforms, and Meta by name, for "enhanced diligence". The same notice has been served on cartoonist Satish Acharya, who lost nine cartoons and then his account, on journalists covering the October protests, and days ago on comedian Kajol Srinivasan. The Union Government applies the pressure and Meta has chosen to answer it with a system that censors first and explains nothing.

IFF will soon challenge Meta's automated restriction system in an appropriate legal proceeding. A joke is not a threat to the nation, and we will not let Meta’s algorithms decide otherwise.

Our demands
1) Meta must restore the post in India, and tell IFF, Aadvik and Pulkit Mani which order, authority and provision it relied on, if any.
2) Meta must suspend the automated restriction of content in India and disclose the inputs on which its "automated system" acts.
3) MeitY must state whether any direction, Sahyog Portal intimation or advisory concerned this cartoon, and withdraw and publish its advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026.
4) The Union Government must restrict content only by reasoned, published orders under Section 69A or by intimations that comply with Rule 3(1)(d), and never by leaning on platforms.

Speak up
A memory hole works only as long as people accept it in silence. If you are a cartoonist, comic, creator or journalist whose post or account has been withheld with this notice, write to us at legal@internetfreedom.in with screenshots of every notice and we will try our best to provide you help pro-bono. Over the past 72 hours we have assisted close to 56 social media users, some of whom had their accounts restored. We are in this together!

INDIA TO IDENTIFY ALL TELEGRAM, WHATSAPP AND SIGNAL USERS WITH "SIM BINDING"

India is set to enforce "SIM binding" for major messaging apps from around January 1, 2027.

What is the ruling

The Department of Telecommunications (@DoT_India) directed platforms including WhatsApp (@WhatsApp), Telegram (@telegram), Signal (@signalapp), Snapchat (@Snapchat), others in 2025 to keep accounts continuously linked to the specific active SIM used for registration.

If that SIM is removed, deactivated or swapped, the app should stop working on the device until the correct SIM is present and verified.

iOS has long blocked apps from directly reading SIM status or hardware identifiers. Apple (@Apple) released a software patch in September that lets apps detect when an iPhone lacks a SIM card, making compliance possible for messaging apps. Apple has not issued a detailed public statement on its reasoning. Earlier queries to the company went unanswered.

What it means for online privacy

The rule does not break end-to-end encryption. It does, however, strengthen the permanent link between a messaging account, a telecom-issued phone number, and the owner's identity.

The Department of Telecommunications runs platforms such as the Digital Intelligence Platform (DIP) and Sanchar Saathi (TAFCOP). These aggregate connection data across operators so authorities can see how SIMs are linked to an individual's verified identity.

Claimed motivation

The government want to identify everyone online.

The government says the rule closes a loophole that lets accounts keep working after the SIM is removed or the number is used from abroad. This has been exploited for phishing, impersonation, "digital arrest" scams and other fraud. Officials cite large cyber-fraud losses and argue that tying accounts to KYC-verified telecom identities improves traceability, similar to existing SIM/device binding already used in banking and UPI (@NPCI_NPCI) apps.

Experts' opinion

Fraudsters routinely obtain SIMs with weak or fake KYC, use them briefly, and discard them. Binding does little against that or against malware, phishing kits and session hijacking.

Industry groups such as IAMAI (@IAMAIForum) have argued the rule mainly creates friction for ordinary users while leaving core attack vectors largely intact,

India's record on using online deanonymising tools

India has a documented pattern of using legal, technical, and policing tools to restrict online speech, target critics, and limit communications during protests—actions frequently criticized by human-rights organisations as disproportionate or politically selective. The new SIM-binding and related telecom identification rules increase the technical capacity to track identity-linked communications, raising the practical risk of similar misuse even if the stated purpose is "fraud prevention".

Reporters Without Borders (@RSF_inter) ranked India 157th out of 180 in its 2026 World Press Freedom Index. RSF and others cite violence against journalists, heavy concentration of media ownership linked to figures close to the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (@BJP4India), and the increasing use of criminal laws against reporters and critics.

Section 69A of the IT Act is the main blocking tool. In 2026, orders have targeted satirical cartoons critical of the prime minister, fact-checker posts, media outlets such as The Wire (@thewire_in), and accounts posting political criticism or mockery.

In October 2026, during demonstrations in Delhi linked to voter-roll revisions and the "Cockroach Janta Party" movement, which criticised the Election Commission (@ECISVEEP), authorities imposed mobile-internet blackouts, conducted mass detentions (including opposition leaders such as Rahul Gandhi and journalists, and reportedly monitored messaging groups.

What can concerned Indians do?

Practical steps for Indians concerned about online privacy are limited by mandatory SIM ID checks, biometric rules, and SIM-binding requirements, but they can still meaningfully reduce exposure.

True anonymity is difficult in India because almost all consumer SIMs are tied to verified identity through ID checks and increasingly biometric checks.

👉 Prefer Signal for sensitive conversations. It has stronger default end-to-end encryption and collects less metadata than WhatsApp. Both will still be subject to SIM-binding, but Signal's design is more privacy-oriented.

👉 Use a reputable no-logs VPN (Mullvad (@mullvadnet), Proton VPN (@ProtonVPN) for sensitive browsing or public Wi-Fi. Note that CERT-In (@IndianCERT) logging rules led most privacy-focused providers to remove physical servers from India; many now offer virtual Indian IPs hosted abroad.

👉 Enable disappearing messages, turn off read receipts where possible, and verify safety numbers for important contacts.

👉 Restrict who can see your phone number, profile photo, last seen, and "about" status (set to "My contacts" or "Nobody").

👉 Avoid using the same number for banking, government services, and casual or sensitive chats if you can manage a second number within the legal 9-SIM limit.

Polymarket has been blocked in India due to legal action by the Indian government. The platform itself hasn't taken any direct action against Indian users.

What happened?

In 2025, India passed the Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act (PROGA), which came into effect on May 1, 2026. The law prohibits real-money online games, including betting and prediction markets. Platforms like Polymarket and Kalshi fall under this category.

1\. On April 25, 2026, India's Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology reportedly directed VPN providers and intermediaries to restrict access to platforms like Polymarket.

2\. By May 2026, ISPs had blocked Polymarket at the DNS level. Many Indian users could no longer access the website.

3\. Polymarket itself didn't list India as a restricted country and had previously allowed users to sign up. However, government restrictions affected access.

4\. In October 2026, Polymarket's official X account was also reportedly withheld in India following a legal demand, preventing many Indian users from viewing its posts.

In short: Polymarket hasn't reportedly taken users' money or frozen their accounts specifically because they are Indian. The restrictions came from the Indian government, which blocked access to the platform and reportedly restricted its X account as well.

text:
📍 Bangalore, India’s First eSIM Box Syndicate Busted by Karnataka Cyber Command; 4 Held After 55-Day Hunt

In a first-of-its-kind operation in India, the Karnataka State Police Cyber Command Unit has dismantled an illegal eSIM box network running from two residential apartments in Whitefield. Four operatives were arrested from Tiroda in Maharashtra’s Gondia district after a nearly 55-day technical investigation.
The probe began on August 26, 2026, after Bharti Airtel’s Chief Circle Nodal Officer flagged suspicious, unauthorized routing over Airtel connections in Whitefield and Kadugodi. Unlike physical SIMs, the syndicate used virtual eSIM profiles, making tracking difficult. Investigators coordinated with the Department of Telecommunications (DoT) to pierce encrypted provisioning networks.
Raids uncovered two operational hubs:
•  Kadugodi: 6 SIM boxes (32 slots each) → 192 active eSIM lines
•  Pattandur Agrahara: 4 SIM boxes (32 slots each) → 128 active lines
Total capacity: 320 live lines acting as an illicit domestic exchange to mask international origins, bypass telecom firewalls, and evade lawful interception.
The setup served as the backbone for nationwide cybercrimes, including “Digital Arrest” scams, sextortion, and high-value financial frauds. Police said preliminary estimates suggest losses running into hundreds of crores.

“The actual number of victims and full extent of the network are still under verification,” said Dr. Pronab Mohanty, IPS, Director General of Police, Cyber Command. Forensic analysis of seized hardware and cloud logs is underway

text:
Laws are meant to protect citizens.

Three legal protections worth examining
1. First Amendment — Freedom of speech and the press
A documentary examining alleged corruption, political influence, corporate conduct, and government accountability generally falls within the category of speech receiving strong constitutional protection.
The Supreme Court has repeatedly recognized that debate on public issues deserves especially robust protection.
2. New York Times Co. v. Sullivan (1964)
If a U.S. defamation claim involves statements about public officials or public figures, the plaintiff generally must establish actual malice: that the defendant published a false statement knowing it was false or with reckless disregard for whether it was true.
This standard can be difficult for plaintiffs to satisfy, although it does not protect knowingly or recklessly false factual allegations.
3. The SPEECH Act (2010)
This federal statute is especially relevant if an Indian court awards defamation damages against you.
It generally prevents enforcement of foreign defamation judgments in U.S. courts unless the foreign law provides protections comparable to the First Amendment and applicable state law, or the defendant would have been liable under U.S. law.
It also provides a potential route to seek a U.S. court declaration that a foreign defamation judgment cannot be enforced domestically, subject to jurisdictional and statutory requirements.

text:
MeitY's advisory to Meta directs the suppression of protest reporting on Instagram and Facebook. It must be withdrawn.

19 Oct 2026

On 10 October 2026, the Cyber Laws Division of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued an advisory to Meta Platforms bearing File No. 6(2)/2026-Cyberlaws. It was not published on the MEITY website and first HT and then PTI reported it on 18 October. Any such advisory is not a legal order and MEITY is not legally empowered to issue them on the basis of any statutory provision. This advisory followed, by two days, an advisory of 8 October to all social media intermediaries calling for "enhanced diligence" over content on "ongoing public events", asking platforms to "label or add context" to misleading content and to "give priority to complaints from authorised Government agencies".  IFF called for the withdrawal of that advisory on 9 October. The Meta advisory was issued on the day the Delhi Police detained protesters and journalists at the demonstrations called over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

The advisory states that content relating to "public-order and law and order situations" is being "prominently displayed and recommended" on Meta's platforms and, "when presented without adequate context or disproportionately amplified", "may contribute to public confusion, apprehension and disturbance of public order and social tranquillity". It singles out "unverified or misleading claims regarding the imposition of emergency, restrictions, police action or other official measures". Further, Meta is advised to review its "recommendation and content ranking mechanisms", to ensure its systems "do not result in disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives", and to furnish "information or assistance" to law enforcement, "with immediate effect". PTI reports that the Ministry acted on inputs from "agencies" that Meta's platforms were not promoting all "narratives" equally.

This advisory matches restrictions on META platforms related to protest content and reporting in the same timline. On 10 October, the Instagram account of Molitics India was withheld in India. On 11 October, a Mathrubhumi English reel showing a woman clinging to a pole as police officers attempted to detain her was restricted citing, "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement", and a video report by Observer Post Hindi was restricted on Facebook by what Meta called an "automated system" acting under the IT Rules, 2021. On 12 October, the Instagram account of journalist Shubhangi Das Gupta was restricted in India for alleged non-compliance with "local IT Rules". On 13 October, the account of Journo Mirror (about five lakh followers) was withheld. The account of Fridays For Future India has since been withheld without any stated reason. Meta's notices to these users do not disclose what is unlawful about the content. 

As per notices shared by us by those who have been censored by META, they take two forms: 

1. "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", and, 

2. "through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements under India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules". 

Neither names the issuing agency, the order, the provision of law or offence the content is said to disclose, or the URL complained of. We know due to litigation that the first notice related to a Sahyog order issued by a Law Enforcement Agency (LEA), while the second one is without any legal order. At the same time, several users received no communication at all. Instagram used the same "automated system" notice against Anjali Priya, Varnika Dhawan and Sachin Gupta after the July protests, and against cartoonist Satish Acharya, who lost nine cartoons and then his account between February and September 2026. 

In April 2026, The Hindu reported that Meta automatically restricts government and police flagged content in India at scale, and seeks a separate government direction before restoring content later found to be legally unsupported. IFF objected to Meta on 4 May 2026. IFF condemns the advisory of 10 October and the restrictions imposed in its wake. An executive communication that instructs a platform to suppress "unverified" claims about "police action" and to correct a "limited set of narratives", issued on the day of a police crackdown and kept from the public, is a censorship directive in all but name.  It makes the State the editor of what Indians may see of a protest against the State. IFF calls upon MeitY to withdraw it and upon Meta to disclose what it has done under it.

Our demands

1. MeitY must withdraw the advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026 forthwith and publish them.

2. MeitY must abandon proposed Rule 3(4) and restrict content only by reasoned, published orders under Section 69A or notices compliant with Rule 3(1)(d).

3. Meta must disclose every takedown, account restriction and act of downranking carried out under the advisories, and its compliance report to the Ministry.

4. Meta must restore the accounts and posts of journalists, outlets and creators restricted since 8 October 2026 unless it holds a valid legal order, and must furnish that order to the person affected.

5. Meta must suspend the automated restriction of content in India and disclose on what inputs its "automated system" acts.

Any person whose account or content has been withheld in India since 8 October 2026 may write to IFF at legal@internetfreedom.in. IFF is providing assistance pro bono.

Rejection of Plaint and Return of Plaint: The Difference

Under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, rejection and return of a plaint are not the same. The distinction lies in the grounds for the order and its legal consequences.

Rejection of Plaint — Order VII Rule 11 CPC

A plaint may be rejected where:

It does not disclose a cause of action.
The relief is undervalued and the plaintiff fails to correct it within the time allowed.
The plaint is insufficiently stamped and the required court fee is not supplied within the time allowed.
The suit appears from the statements in the plaint to be barred by law.
The plaint is not filed in duplicate.
The plaintiff fails to comply with Order VII Rule 9 CPC.

Rejection of a plaint amounts to a decree under Section 2(2) CPC and is appealable under Section 96 CPC. Order VII Rule 13 also makes clear that rejection does not, by itself, bar the filing of a fresh plaint, subject to limitation and other legal requirements.

Return of Plaint — Order VII Rule 10 CPC

A plaint is returned when it is to be presented before the court in which the suit ought to have been instituted. This commonly arises where the court lacks territorial or pecuniary jurisdiction. Questions of subject-matter jurisdiction must be dealt with under the applicable law.

An order returning a plaint is appealable under Order XLIII Rule 1(a) CPC, subject to the applicable procedure, including Order VII Rule 10A where relevant.

The practical distinction is important: rejection is governed by Order VII Rule 11; return is governed by Order VII Rule 10. The applicable provision determines the nature of the order and the remedy available to the aggrieved party.

The SC in E.M.T.S. Ltd. v. Afdin Ventures Ltd. (2026) 16 NWLR (Pt. 2066) 447 eruditely ordained that Order 6 rule 3(5) of the Supreme Court Rules, 2024, which requires an appellant to file evidence of payment of all sums ordered by way of costs into an escrow account in the name of the Chief Registrar within 21 days of filing the notice of appeal, is couched in mandatory terms, and non-compliance renders the appeal liable to dismissal. However, notwithstanding the appellant’s failure to comply with this requirement and to obey the trial court’s order to deposit the judgment sum, which rendered the respondent’s preliminary objection meritorious, the Court is compelled not to terminate the appeal, SOLELY because proceedings for the enforcement of arbitral awards are sui generis, possessing a peculiar commercial character and significance, and are not ordinary civil disputes. Consequently, the preliminary objection was overruled, and the Court proceeded to determine the appeal on its merits pursuant to section 22 of the Supreme Court Act.

Exemption from Liability of Intermediaries in Certain Cases

Section 79 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 provides legal protection to intermediaries against liability for third-party content hosted or transmitted through their platforms.

An intermediary includes social media platforms, internet service providers, web-hosting companies, search engines, and similar online service providers. Examples include X (Twitter), Facebook, and YouTube.

Sub-section (1)

An intermediary shall not be liable for any third-party information, data, or communication link made available or hosted by it, subject to the conditions specified in the Act.

Sub-section (2)

This protection applies only if:

The intermediary's role is limited to providing access to a communication system through which information is transmitted, temporarily stored, or hosted;

The intermediary does not initiate the transmission;

The intermediary does not select the receiver of the transmission;

The intermediary does not select or modify the information contained in the transmission; and

The intermediary observes due diligence and complies with the requirements prescribed under the Act and the applicable rules.

Sub-section (3)

The protection under Section 79 shall not apply if:

1. The intermediary has conspired, abetted, aided, or induced the commission of an unlawful act; or

2. Upon receiving actual knowledge, or upon being notified by the appropriate Government or its agency that any information, data, or communication link hosted on its computer resource is being used to commit an unlawful act, the intermediary fails to expeditiously remove or disable access to such material while preserving evidence.

Explanation

The term “Third Party Information” refers to any information dealt with by an intermediary in its capacity as an intermediary.

Practical Significance

Section 79 provides a “safe Harbour” to intermediaries. As a result, social media platforms and other intermediaries are generally not automatically liable for content posted by their users. However, if they participate in unlawful activities or fail to act after receiving a valid legal notice or government direction, they may lose the protection granted under Section 79.

The scope of this provision was further clarified by the Supreme Court of India in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India. The Court held that “Actual knowledge” for the purposes of Section 79 generally arises through a court order or a notification issued by a competent government authority, requiring the intermediary to take appropriate action.

"arXiv:2610.37571v1 [https://t.co/gQRNwvACTl] 27 Oct 2026
TeamGym: A Gym for Team Decision-Making by AI Agents with Distributed Information
Chanwoo ParkJaywoong JeongZachary WojtowiczYubin KimTaekyun LeeKaiqing ZhangAsuman OzdaglarMIT KAIST UT Austin University of Maryland⋆Equal contribution.Abstract
Many real-world decisions require teams to integrate information distributed across participants. Yet AI agents are still primarily trained and benchmarked in isolation. We introduce TeamGym, an environment for evaluating and training language model-based agents on team decision-making problems constructed from real-world legal, finance, medical, and software engineering corpora. TeamGym introduces a method to identify a minimal set of facts, each element of which is necessary and all of which are collectively sufficient for a correct final decision, which we call pivotal information. This enables TeamGym to both control the distribution of pivotal information and track how well agents identify and integrate pivotal information when making team decisions. Examining 8 language models on 12 source corpora, we find that current AI agents often fail to effectively share information: Distributing pivotal information across participants lowers success rate by 22.9 percentage points on average relative to giving the same information to a single model (a communication gap). We also document that participants do not effectively retrieve decision-relevant information on their own: A team’s success rate is lowered by a further 19.9 points when participants must identify and extract pivotal information from source material rather than receiving it directly (a retrieval gap). To help remedy these deficits, we use TeamGym to train policies through reinforcement learning on team decision loss. Across two policy-training experiments, we find that training improves final-decision quality and induces emergent coordination in participation, speaker selection, and communication, even though the reward evaluates only the final decision.Fig. 1:TeamGym overview. TeamGym distributes pivotal information across participants, structures evidence exchange during team interaction, and evaluates the resulting decision. Its controlled conditions separate communication and retrieval gaps, while the training loop supports configurable policy optimization.

1Introduction
The frontier of AI is turning to multi-agent systems, in which AI agents are organized into teams that communicate to solve problems (Li et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2023; Hong et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2026a). Yet AI models are still trained and benchmarked largely as individual agents, which raises the question of whether they acquire the capacities and dispositions needed to be effective teammates. In human groups, collective intelligence, which is linked to social sensitivity and turn-taking, predicts team performance better than individual intelligence (Woolley et al., 2010). Although AI agents differ from humans, this finding motivates evaluating them as teams rather than only as individuals.A central challenge in team decision-making is that decision-relevant information is typically distributed across members. Reaching a collective decision requires members to identify and retrieve relevant information, communicate it efficiently, and integrate it into a final decision. Team theory has long studied this challenge (Radner, 1962; Marschak and Radner, 1972), while empirical research on human group decision-making finds that people often struggle to identify and integrate critical private information (Stasser and Titus, 1985; Lu et al., 2012).We introduce TeamGym, a gym for constructing team decision problem instances from source corpora, and for evaluating and training participant and coordinator policies under controlled information distributions and communication structures. TeamGym targets questions that existing benchmarks and multi-agent systems leave open. Single-agent benchmarks measure individual model capabilities (Wu et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024), while research on multi-agent LLM systems focuses on designing harnesses that solve a given problem (Li et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2023; Hong et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2026b). Neither offers much evidence on whether participants can retrieve and communicate decision-relevant information, how team performance varies with information distribution and communication structure, or whether training can improve participant and coordinator policies.
1.0.0.1 Method.
TeamGym constructs controlled team decision problem instances from real-world source corpora. For each instance, it derives a decision objective from one or more corpus questions and either retains a corpus-provided reference decision or constructs one from corpus annotations and source materials. Source annotations and reasoning associated with the reference decision guide the selection of candidate evidence units, such as sentences, paragraphs, tables, or code blocks. Source-specific grounding and model-based complete-set and leave-one-out checks retain units that together support the reference decision but whose individual removal leaves it unsupported or unresolved. These retained units are pivotal information units (PIUs) and collectively form the instance’s pivotal information.Holding the problem instance and its pivotal information fixed, TeamGym can vary who initially has each PIU (the PIU distribution), whether participants receive PIUs directly or source material containing them, the communication structure, and token budgets. The team collectively receives the pivotal information, but the evidence is distributed across participants to make communication necessary for a fully supported final decision. The communication structure specifies whether a coordinator controls communication, how speakers are selected, and which decision maker makes the final decision. Token budgets constrain what decision makers may observe and generate. To understand what reduces team performance, we define two success-rate gaps. The communication gap is the drop when the same PIUs are distributed across participants rather than given to one model. The retrieval gap is the further drop when the team must retrieve those PIUs from source material rather than receive them directly. Beyond evaluation, TeamGym supports training participant and coordinator policies under controlled PIU distributions, communication structures, and token budgets.Table 1:Source corpora and decisions. The problem instances constructed from the source corpora use different source materials and decision objectives across four domains.DomainSource corporaDecisionsLegalCUAD, MAUD, eCFR Casebook,MSLR, Multi-LexSum, SARAContract profiles, merger reviews, compliance and enforcement,legal and procedural conclusions, and tax calculationsFinanceFinDVer, FinLongDocQASEC-filing findings, calculations, comparisons, and classificationsMedicalMLCR, EvidenceBenchEvidence-grounded medical reviews and biomedical answersSoftwareengineeringSWE Atlas–Codebase QnA, DeepSWECodebase QA and multi-turn, long-horizon repository-levelcode repair with functionally evaluated patches
We construct problem instances from source corpora in Table 1 (Hendrycks et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2023b; Office of the Federal Register, 2026a; Office of the Federal Register, 2026b; Yu et al., 2027; Shen et al., 2022; Holzenberger et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2026; Wisedocs, 2026; Wang et al., 2025; Raghavendra et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026). Source materials include contracts, regulations, SEC filings, biomedical papers, and source code, while the decision formats are finite-choice, written, and numeric.
1.0.0.2 Findings.
The resulting comparisons hold the problem instance and pivotal information fixed to isolate communication and retrieval effects from differences in problem difficulty. (1) Across eight language models and 12 source corpora, the decision success rate is 22.9 percentage points lower when the same PIUs are distributed across a team than when one model receives them all, and a further 19.9 points lower when the same team must retrieve its PIUs from source material rather than receiving them directly. (2) Across domains, differences in the success rate among communication structures vary across PIU-distribution conditions. For example, across the six legal source corpora when participants receive PIUs directly, sequential communication in which each speaker selects the next participant leads simultaneous communication by 3.9 points when one PIU is initially common to the team, but trails it by 9.8 points when the team includes an additional participant without a PIU, corresponding to a 13.8-point change in the difference between their success rates. (3) Optimizing final-decision quality changes the communication process itself. With coordinator control, joint two-policy training produces a compact, exhaustive information-elicitation protocol; without a coordinator, training the shared participant policy improves end-to-end final-decision quality and completion and induces emergent coordination in participation, speaker selection, and communication. Tracing PIUs through these trajectories shows that increased participation makes more pivotal information available on FinDVer validation, but not on held-out FinLongDocQA.TeamGym therefore provides a controlled environment in which team decision-making capabilities can be evaluated and trained under different information distributions and communication structures.
2Related Work

2.0.0.1 Team decision theory and organizational economics.
Team decision theory studies cooperative decision makers with a team objective and a decentralized information structure. A team problem couples a shared objective with an information structure and one policy for each decision maker (Radner, 1962; Marschak and Radner, 1972; Yüksel and Başar, 2013). Classical analysis largely studies the properties of different computation structures and policies, not how they can be learned and implemented computationally. Under tractable joint-policy optimization (A1), computing this collection is assumed feasible before execution, although the exact problem can be intractable even in finite-horizon decentralized control (Bernstein et al., 2002). TeamGym instead evaluates and trains language-model policies, comparing policy collections before and after training under the same conditions.
2.0.0.2 Mechanism design.
Under the direct-report mechanism assumption (A2), mechanism design represents private information as a type that can be elicited directly under the applicable equilibrium assumptions, and that participants know their type and can communicate it if they so choose (Maskin and Sjostrom, 2002; Myerson, 1979; Myerson, 2008). In practice, however, attention and cognitive limitations constrain agent’s ability to identify, extract, and communicate information contained in long source material, even if it is in principle available to them (Mookherjee, 2006). TeamGym assumes a shared team payoff and studies bounded natural-language messages derived from source material.
2.0.0.3 Communication constraints.
Research in organizational economics, planning, and reinforcement learning examines communication costs and message limits (Cremer et al., 2007; Wu et al., 2011; Kim et al., 2019; Zhu et al., 2024). The idealization of nonbinding communication resources (A3) permits decision makers to access and transmit relevant information without binding observation or message constraints. TeamGym instead makes its resource budgets explicit.We defer additional related work on multistage communication, human-AI and group decision making, multi-agent LLM systems, benchmark contrasts, and the source corpora to Section 6.
3TeamGym Environment

3.1Decision Problem and Communication
We formalize TeamGym as a finite-horizon team decision problem (Radner, 1962; Marschak and Radner, 1972; Yüksel and Başar, 2013; Nayyar et al., 2013). A problem instance q fixes underlying source materials, a decision objective, a decision format, a set 𝒟q of possible final decisions, and a problem-specific evaluator that assigns each d∈𝒟q a team payoff Uq​(d)∈[0,1]. A decision maker is a role whose policy may generate a query, send a message, or make the final decision. A participant is a decision maker that may send messages during communication. A coordinator is a decision maker that may control communication by selecting or querying participants and may make the final decision. Initially, each participant receives an initial local observation, while all decision makers receive the same initial common observation containing the decision objective and decision format. The policy ρi maps the information currently available to decision maker i to a distribution over the queries, messages, or final decisions permitted for its role; ρ denotes the collection of decision-maker policies. The communication structure 𝒞 specifies whether a coordinator controls communication, which participants may send messages and when, whether messages are sequential or simultaneous, and which decision maker makes the final decision. The resource budgets B, including token budgets, constrain what decision makers may observe and generate and how often participants may send messages. Queries and messages form the communication transcript; a decision maker’s local transcript is the portion available to it under 𝒞 and B. The initial local and common observations, together with the observation rules induced by 𝒞 and the observation limits in B, define the decentralized information structure. An episode is one complete execution through the final-decision stage for fixed q, initial observations, 𝒞, B, and ρ. For these fixed inputs, the resulting interaction induces a distribution over final decisions, and we evaluate ρ by its expected team payoff, 𝔼​[Uq​(d)]. Holding q and the initial observations fixed while varying 𝒞, B, or ρ changes the interaction conditions without changing the problem instance.For evaluation, we consider five communication structures (Figure 2), each proceeding in scheduled steps called communication rounds: (1) Round robin, under which one participant sends a message per round in a fixed cyclic order; (2) Current-speaker selection, which starts with the first participant in that order, after which each speaker selects the next participant; (3) Simultaneous responses, under which all participants respond in one round; (4) Coordinator-selected speaker, under which the coordinator selects and queries one participant per round; and (5) Broadcast query, under which the coordinator sends the same query to all participants, whose responses are generated in the same round. In Round robin, Current-speaker selection, and Simultaneous responses, no coordinator controls communication, and a separate final decision maker that does not participate in communication reads the complete communication transcript and makes the final decision. In Coordinator-selected speaker and Broadcast query, the coordinator controls communication and makes the final decision. Appendix C provides message-generation and implementation details and connections to prior work.Fig. 2:Communication structures (𝒞). The three structures on the left have no coordinator and use a separate final decision maker. In the two structures on the right, a coordinator controls interaction and makes the final decision. The rule below each panel specifies who may send messages in each communication round.
One participant sends a message per round in a fixed cyclic order.The first participant starts; each speaker selects the next participant.All participants respond in the same round.The coordinator selects and queries one participant per round.The coordinator sends the same query to all participants, who respond in the same round.
3.2Problem-Instance Construction and Evaluation
TeamGym constructs each problem instance q from one source corpus using materials such as contracts, SEC filings, biomedical papers, or source code. Each q is paired with a reference decision dref supported by its source materials and used in construction and evaluation. For each q, we identify an inclusion-minimal set ℐqmin={i1,…,ik} called its pivotal information; each ij is a pivotal information unit (PIU). Informally, this information is sufficient to determine a final decision that achieves the highest possible team payoff, whereas removing any one PIU leaves insufficient information to guarantee such a decision. Because DeepSWE admits multiple valid patches and costly repository execution, it instead uses functional PIUs validated under a fixed, bounded protocol (Appendix D.6.4). Appendix D.1 formalizes this definition.
3.2.0.1 PIU construction.
When a model’s reasoning trace used to produce dref is available, we retain it; otherwise, we generate reasoning conditioned on dref, following answer-conditioned rationale generation (Wang et al., 2023a). To identify ℐqmin, we use source annotations and the retained or generated reasoning to locate candidate units in the source materials. Grounding and model-based checks then test whether the candidates together support dref and whether removing any one leaves the final decision unsupported or unresolved. The candidates retained by these checks form ℐqmin. We then verify that a model given all pivotal information can solve each evaluated problem instance (Section 4.1). Appendix D.7 reports an additional re-check of PIU necessity on representative instances using a model not used for construction.📷Fig. 3:PIU construction and allocation. Candidate evidence units are grounded in the source material, checked for joint sufficiency and leave-one-out necessity, and retained as an inclusion-minimal pivotal-information set. The resulting PIUs can then be allocated across participants while preserving the decision task and reference decision.

3.2.0.2 PIU distribution.
A PIU distribution specifies who initially has each PIU in ℐqmin: a PIU may be assigned to one or more participants through their initial local observations or placed in the initial common observation shared by the team. Figure 4 defines and illustrates five conditions. For a fixed q, the conditions vary the PIU distribution while keeping the pivotal information and dref unchanged. The initial common observation may also include participant descriptions, which summarize participants’ subject matter or function without revealing their assigned PIUs and can inform speaker selection.Fig. 4:Five PIU-distribution conditions. Each condition distributes the ℐqmin across the initial local and common observations without changing q or dref. Colored boxes denote distinct PIUs, and ∅ denotes a participant assigned no PIU. The common-observation panel marks information initially visible to the full team. Not every problem instance admits every condition.
One PIU per participant.Some PIUs are shared by two https://t.co/ciw2yZHgJs participant per PIU, plus one participant without a https://t.co/8YWGCljus0 PIU is common to all participants; the other PIUs remain https://t.co/y6sZuoW5jk participant receives all but one PIU; another receives the remaining PIU.
3.2.0.3 Source-material distribution.
Rather than receiving PIUs directly, participants’ initial observations may contain portions of the contracts, filings, papers, or source code used to construct q. We divide this source material into units without dividing a PIU, assign PIU-containing units according to the fixed PIU distribution, and distribute the remaining units across participants. For every problem instance, we then verify that no participant can produce a correct final decision from its initial local observation and the initial common observation. Appendix D.7 reports an additional re-check of this requirement on representative instances using a model not used for construction. Appendix D provides the formal source terminology and source-specific construction and distribution procedures.
3.2.0.4 Evaluation.
A problem family groups problem instances constructed from the same source corpus that require the same general kind of work and use the same evaluation procedure. For a problem family with a binary success criterion, episode success rate is the proportion of episodes whose final decisions succeed. Depending on the problem family, final decisions are compared with reference decisions or assessed by an LLM judge using problem-specific criteria. Software-engineering patches are checked by an official repository verifier.
4Evaluation with TeamGym
We evaluate LLMs on problem instances constructed from legal, finance, medical, and software-engineering source corpora under three evaluation conditions: (1) Single-Agent All-PIU, in which one model receives all PIUs and makes the final decision; (2) Multi-Agent PIU-Only, in which the PIUs are distributed directly across participants; and (3) Multi-Agent Full-Context, in which the same participants instead receive source material containing their assigned PIUs. For each problem instance and LLM, the three conditions share the same PIUs and evaluator; the two multi-agent conditions also share the same PIU distribution, communication structure, and resource budgets.Figure 5 summarizes how the information available to the decision maker changes across these three conditions and shows the corresponding aggregate communication and retrieval gaps.📷Fig. 5:Three evaluation conditions and aggregate performance gaps. Single-Agent All-PIU provides all pivotal information to one model; Multi-Agent PIU-Only distributes those PIUs across participants; and Multi-Agent Full-Context embeds the same PIUs in participants’ source materials. The communication gap compares the first two conditions, and the retrieval gap compares the two multi-agent conditions.

4.1Problem Instances
Table 1 summarizes the source corpora and decisions, while Table 2 reports the constructed and evaluated problem-instance counts. Before evaluation, we perform repeated checks in which GPT-5.5 receives all PIUs under Single-Agent All-PIU. It succeeds under the problem-specific evaluator at least once on every evaluated problem instance, verifying that a model given all pivotal information can solve the instance before the PIUs are distributed (Section 3.2). Appendix D reports additional construction details and problem-instance statistics for each source corpus.Table 2:Problem-instance counts across four domains and twelve source corpora.LegalFinance, medical, and software engineeringSource corpusConstructedproblem instancesEvaluatedproblem instancesDomainSource corpusConstructedproblem instancesEvaluatedproblem instancesCUAD53830FinanceFinDVer38930MAUD55730FinLongDocQA24930eCFR Casebook1818MedicalMLCR2929MSLR1111EvidenceBench4545Multi-LexSum2929SoftwareengineeringSWE Atlas–Codebase QnA3232SARA4545DeepSWE1212

4.2Cross-Domain Communication and Retrieval Gaps
For this cross-domain comparison, both multi-agent conditions use One PIU per participant (Figure 4) and Coordinator-selected speaker. The communication gap is the decrease in episode success rate from Single-Agent All-PIU to Multi-Agent PIU-Only, and the retrieval gap is the additional decrease from Multi-Agent PIU-Only to Multi-Agent Full-Context. With the model and problem instance fixed, larger gaps indicate greater difficulty communicating and integrating distributed PIUs (communication gap) and retrieving them from source material (retrieval gap), rather than differences in model knowledge. The retrieval contrast corresponds to a departure from A2, and the communication contrast corresponds to a departure from A3. Figure 6 reports the episode success rates used to compute these gaps. “They sent him to Ghana, with full knowledge that Ghana is systematically deporting refugees back to the very countries they fled,” says immigration attorney Meredyth Yoon.

60 Minutes obtained the names of all the people on a flight that left Texas on July 30th and took deportees to three countries in Africa, including Ghana.  Of the 19 deportees 60 Minutes reached who were sent to Ghana, 17 say they were then transported against their will to countries U.S. immigration judges ruled they should not be returned to. Moussa Diawara was one of them. The Department of Homeland Security told 60 Minutes that Ghana had provided the U.S. with “diplomatic assurances for [Diawara’s] safety.”

Yoon says the U.S. government was warned about Ghana’s conduct in a lawsuit last year. Despite this, the U.S. sent 10 more flights to Ghana, which Yoon believes is a violation of international law. https://t.co/M1eBc81YI7

Context and Breakdown

The excerpt comes from a 60 Minutes investigation into the U.S. government's "third-country deportation" agreements. Fact-checking this requires separating verified administrative facts, self-reported testimonies, legal definitions under the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA), and conflicting government vs. advocate positions.

Claim 1: Diawara and others were "refugees" whom judges ruled could not be deported

Rating: Misleading / Legal Conflation

The Legal Distinction: The claim conflates refugee/asylee status with Withholding of Removal. Moussa Diawara was never granted asylum or recognized as a refugee under U.S. law. An immigration judge granted him "Withholding of Removal" under 8 U.S.C. § 1231(b)(3).

Country-Specific Relief: Unlike asylum, Withholding of Removal is strictly country-specific. It prohibits deportation solely to the specific country where the alien demonstrated a probability of persecution (in Diawara’s case, Mali).
Statutory Third-Country Authority: Under INA § 241(b)(2), an alien subject to a final removal order who cannot be sent to their primary country may be removed to any willing third country. The U.S. immigration judge’s 2012 order explicitly allowed DHS to deport Diawara to an alternative safe country. While the U.S. cannot lawfully deport him directly to Mali, deporting him to Ghana does not inherently violate an immigration judge's order under U.S. statutory law.
Claim 2: 17 of 19 deportees reached by 60 Minutes were sent against their will back to barred countries

Rating: Supported by CBS Investigation, but Relies on Self-Reported Accounts

The CBS Sample: 60 Minutes confirmed it obtained the flight manifest from the July 30 deportation flight carrying 63 individuals. The reporting team contacted 19 of those sent to Ghana; 17 stated they were forcibly put on planes by Ghanaian authorities back to their countries of origin (including Mali, Niger, and Guinea).

Physical Evidence: Diawara produced DHS-issued baggage tags and medication sheets originating from the U.S. that listed "Mali" as the destination, which Diawara argued showed U.S. complicity in his onward removal.

The DHS Defense: DHS’s top attorney, James Percival, called the baggage tag destination a "clerical error," denied that the U.S. sent Diawara to Mali, and maintained that DHS was unaware of any deportees being forcibly sent by Ghana to other nations against their will.
Claim 3: The U.S. sent deportees "with full knowledge" and in violation of international law
Rating: Contested / Legally Complex

The Advocate’s Case (Chain Refoulement): Under Article 33 of the 1951 Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees and Article 3 of the UN Convention Against Torture (CAT), the principle of non-refoulement forbids sending an individual to a country where they face persecution or torture. International law also prohibits indirect or chain refoulement—deporting someone to a third country knowing that country will expel them to the prohibited territory. Attorney Meredyth Yoon argues that because a 2025 class-action lawsuit warned DHS of Ghana’s practices, DHS acted with constructive knowledge.

The Government’s Legal Shield (Diplomatic Assurances): Under U.S. regulations governing CAT and removal (8 C.F.R. § 1208.18(c)), the Secretary of Homeland Security may rely on formal diplomatic assurances from a receiving government to determine that an individual is not likely to be tortured or transferred unlawfully. DHS confirmed that Ghana provided formal diplomatic assurances for Diawara's safety.

Current Status in U.S. Courts: Lower federal courts have ruled that the administration's third-country deportation procedures violated statutory due process protections. However, the U.S. Supreme Court issued an emergency stay permitting the third-country flights to continue pending a final merits review. As a matter of U.S. domestic law, the flights were operating under active Supreme Court authorization.

Claim 4: DHS sent 10 more flights to Ghana despite warnings
Rating: True
The U.S. government continued deportation flights to Ghana after lawsuits were filed challenging third-country removals.

DHS justified this on two grounds:
The administration's position that it has statutory obligations under the INA to execute final removal orders against noncitizens who lack lawful status.
The Supreme Court lifted lower-court injunctions, granting the executive branch legal latitude to carry out third-country agreements while litigation proceeds.

Additional Fact-Check: Public Safety and Flight Demographics

The political dispute over these flights centers on criminal history versus humanitarian obligations:

Administration Framing: DHS repeatedly characterized these deportations as essential for public safety, removing individuals it labeled serious threats to American communities.
CBS Record Audit: 60 Minutes reviewed criminal records for the 63 deportees aboard the July 30 flight. The data showed:
19% had charges or convictions for crimes (including assault, theft, drugs, or weapons).
19% had only traffic violations.
62% had no criminal record at all.
Moussa Diawara had lived in the U.S. for 25 years with no criminal record, having overstayed a visitor visa. In response to the broadcast, DHS challenged the underlying validity of his claim, asserting that his asylum arguments contained contradictions.

A simple "I accept" checkbox won't save you under the DPDP Act. 

Most platforms treat consent like a formality, but DPDP changes the rules:

- Purpose Limitation: Blanket consent is out. Purpose must be specific and explicit.
- Defined Timelines: No indefinite data holding. You must state the exact duration.
- Right to Withdraw & Erase: If a user withdraws consent or asks for data erasure, processing must stop, and data must be purged immediately.

A basic cookie banner is only 1% of compliance. Real consent management requires full lifecycle governance.

WELCOME BACK TO 1975? IS INDIA WITNESSING A NEW ERA OF DIGITAL CENSORSHIP?

“Say goodbye to freedom of speech.” This is the warning raised by The Unedited Media amid reports of social-media posts and accounts being blocked in India.

The concern is serious. Reports have documented restrictions affecting political cartoonist Satish Acharya, cartoons critical of the Election Commission, and other journalistic content. Acharya's Instagram account was restricted in India again on 20 October 2026, after an earlier restriction in September. Scroll reported that the platform cited legal requirements but the specific reason for the latest restriction remained unclear.

The wider picture is equally troubling. The Indian Express reported nearly 1.95 lakh government-backed blocking orders sent to Instagram, Facebook and YouTube between March and July 2026. These are orders, not a count of individual posts or proven cases of unlawful censorship.

The question is not whether the government can lawfully restrict genuinely unlawful content. The question is whether the powers are being exercised transparently, proportionately and with meaningful safeguards against the silencing of legitimate criticism.

When posts concerning the Election Commission, public institutions or government actions become inaccessible, citizens deserve to know:

🔹 Which authority ordered the restriction?

🔹 What specific law and reasons justified it?

🔹 Was the material independently reviewed before removal?

🔹 Can the affected journalist, cartoonist or citizen challenge the decision effectively?

🔹 Who ensures that legitimate dissent is not swept away by automated compliance?

A democracy cannot thrive if citizens are free to speak only when their words please those in power.

Criticism of the government is not automatically misinformation. Political satire is not automatically unlawful. And a legal notice should not become a substitute for transparent justification and accountability.

The government may cite public order and legal compliance. Those explanations must be examined—not blindly accepted or dismissed. Each restriction deserves scrutiny under the law, with due process and protection for constitutionally guaranteed freedom of expression.

1975 must remain a warning, not a precedent for the digital age.

Share this discussion. Defend independent journalism. Demand transparency. Protect the right to dissent.

text:
Elon, I always admired you until now. I think it would be good for you to end this tweet series ASAP before it becomes impossible to dig yourself out of this mess. Indians were with you thus far, but now you might have triggered an event that will turn them against you. If it was your advisors who made you do this, start by firing them!

Now let’s get into the details :

The claim that Starlink still has “no license” after years of compliance is not accurate. The company received its GMPCS licence in June 2025 and IN-SPACe authorisation in July 2025. What remains is the Ministry of Home Affairs security assessment—covering Indian gateways, data localisation, lawful interception and the ability to restrict service in sensitive areas—and that same assessment is also pending for Reliance’s Jio Satellite and Bharti-backed OneWeb. All three licensed operators are at broadly the same stage. 

Framing the delay as Ambani acting as “real boss” or “Prime Minister,” and dismissing Indian pushback as an “army of shills,” therefore misstates the process and has been widely received as an attack on sovereignty rather than a serious regulatory argument.

For Americans and Musk supporters, this public campaign was unnecessary and has likely made Starlink’s position harder, not easier. India already has some of the world’s cheapest mobile data, produced by real competition between Jio and Airtel. Starlink’s commercial case in that market depends on clearing the same security rules as the other licensees and then offering a price people will actually pay. 

Aggressive personal attacks and inaccurate licence claims have alienated many Indians who were otherwise open to more options in underserved areas. Every major country protects critical communications infrastructure on national-security grounds—the United States does so with Chinese firms, and China does so with Starlink itself. Selective outrage undermines the case for open markets.

Indians are right to be frustrated by the tone and the implication that their government is simply an oligarch’s instrument. Security rules exist for documented reasons and apply equally; they are not a personal favour to any one company. 

At the same time, fixed-broadband penetration remains low and large parts of the country still lack reliable connectivity. If Starlink or any other operator completes the security reviews that already cover all three licensees and then competes on price and performance, allowing that competition is in users’ interest. The process should stay rule-based rather than driven by public insults or political pressure.

The practical path is straightforward: complete the outstanding security assessments on equal terms, assign spectrum fairly, and let the market decide. Misstatements about licences and personalised attacks have only made that outcome more difficult for everyone.

text:
Elon’s claim has two parts. Both fail when you look at the numbers.

“Affordable… for those who can’t afford current prices” 

Starlink’s own India listing says that the service will cost ₹8,600 for a month, plus a one-time hardware kit of about ₹34,000. 

I pay ₹699 for 100 Mbps. Unlimited. 

Indian broadband is very cheap. 

Jio Fiber and Airtel Xstream start in the ₹400–800 range. 

Mobile data is around ₹8 a GB, down from roughly ₹300 a GB in 2014. 

India already has among the cheapest data in the world, which is why internet subscriptions >1.09 billion in 2026.

A household that cannot pay ₹399 for fibre will not pay ₹8,600 plus a ₹34,000 dish. 

Starlink is a premium product. Calling it the affordable option funny. 

“Those who don’t have a connection at all”

5G already covers about 86% of the population and 99.9% of districts. 

I agree, Rural internet subscriptions are the weak spot, 48 per 100 people against 127 urban, but that gap is mostly handset cost, electricity, and last-mile economics, not an absence of towers. 

4G signal is already reported in the large majority of villages. The places Starlink actually fits are the ones fibre and towers will not reach at a rational cost, high Himalayan posts, islands, forest interiors, ships, planes, disaster sites. 

That is a useful complement. It is not “connectivity for India.”

India can build the analogue. ISRO, NSIL and private launch capacity are not a Bangladesh or a Kenya problem. Letting a foreign LEO operator become the rural default freezes demand that should pull an Indian constellation. 

OneWeb (Bharti) and Jio Satellite already hold the same class of licence. (I understand SpaceX is way ahead of these chapus)

Indian telecom supports about 4 million direct and indirect jobs, after a decade of consolidation three operators have servived and on a thin* margins. 

Starlink can serve a few hard-to-reach pockets at a price only institutions, ships, planes and wealthy households will pay, under license terms India writes and can revoke. 

(For Indian Context only)

The Supreme Court has issued notice to the Union Government on a constitutional challenge brought by 21 major news publishers against India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act.
THE QUESTION IS NOT WHETHER PRIVACY MUST BE PROTECTED. THE QUESTION IS WHETHER PRIVACY CAN BE USED TO PREVENT THE EXPOSURE OF WRONGDOING.

Imagine a journalist investigating corruption being required to obtain consent from the very person whose conduct is under investigation.

SINCE WHEN DID THE SUBJECT OF AN INVESTIGATION ACQUIRE A VETO OVER THE INVESTIGATION ITSELF?

Article 19(1)(a) protects freedom of expression and the press. Article 21 protects the fundamental right to privacy.

NEITHER FUNDAMENTAL RIGHT IS A WEAPON FOR THE DESTRUCTION OF THE OTHER.

Privacy must protect human dignity. It must not become a convenient hiding place for corruption, abuse of public office or wrongdoing.

A LAW THAT PROTECTS PERSONAL DATA IS NECESSARY. A LAW THAT COULD MAKE INVESTIGATIVE JOURNALISM DEPENDENT UPON THE PERMISSION OF THOSE UNDER SCRUTINY DESERVES THE STRICTEST CONSTITUTIONAL EXAMINATION.

But press freedom also carries responsibility.

A JOURNALIST IS NOT ABOVE THE RIGHT TO PRIVACY. AND A POWERFUL INDIVIDUAL MUST NOT BE PLACED ABOVE LEGITIMATE PUBLIC SCRUTINY.

The Constitution demands a balance governed by necessity, proportionality and the public interest.

THE PRESS MUST NOT BECOME A PRISONER OF CONSENT. PRIVACY MUST NOT BECOME A CASUALTY OF SENSATIONALISM.

And let the Republic remember:

A DEMOCRACY DOES NOT SURVIVE MERELY BECAUSE ITS CITIZENS CAN SPEAK. IT SURVIVES BECAUSE THEY CAN DISCOVER AND PUBLISH THE TRUTH.

PROTECT PRIVACY. PROTECT JOURNALISM. NEVER SACRIFICE THE CONSTITUTION TO PROTECT EITHER.

text:
No reliable independent data yields a precise factual percentage on Elon Musk’s overall statement follow-throughs; criteria and tracking vary widely.

For the March 2024 promise: Yes. X rolled it out in early April 2024. Accounts with 2500+ verified (Premium-paying) followers received complimentary Premium features (incl. blue check); 5000+ got Premium+. Thousands of influential users received it. Official help pages no longer list it as active for new accounts.

Used Grok bot and was given the following:

Yes, the free Premium promise did happen. Musk posted it on March 28, 2024, and X started handing out free blue checks late on April 3, 2024. Recipients got a notice calling them "an influential member of the community." X never said how many accounts got one. Plenty of journalists and other prominent people did, and several made it clear they didn't want it:
Marcy Wheeler (journalist): "I've been forcibly bluechecked."
Lauren Goode (Wired): "I am not paying Eln Msk for this."
Edward Lucas (UK parliamentary candidate) hid his checkmark. About a week later X announced it was removing the option to hide it.
Some CNBC reporters were also on the receiving end.
Sources: The Verge, CNBC, Guardian, NBC, AP, and India Today for the hide-option change. I found no credible reporting that X ended the program, and I couldn't check X's help pages because the site blocked me.

On how often Musk follows through, there's no single official percentage. The best study puts on-time delivery at roughly 1 in 5.
NYT, June 2026 checked 602 dated business goals Musk posted on X or stated on Tesla earnings calls. About 19% were met as stated and on time. About 35% were late or never delivered, 33% were too vague to verify, and 13% are still in the future. His hit rate has also fallen: in 2015 he met nearly three-quarters of his goals, but fewer than half of his 2020 goals were met on time.
https://t.co/ydD1cr40Gr is an independent open dataset of 339 claims. It found 15% on time, 22% late, 24% missed, and 31% still open.
https://t.co/ydPuACwn7w gives a 22.5% "trust score," but it's a hand-picked, openly hostile collection and says itself that it isn't statistically representative.
So @grok's reply that no reliable percentage exists is out of date. The NYT's 19% is the strongest number to cite.

The Henry Classification System: Still Named After the Man Who Plagiarised It. 

British Plagiarism, Theft and Dishonesty: How Edward Henry Stole the Fingerprint System and Was Rewarded for It. 

In the 1890s the Bengal Police needed a workable method to file and search large numbers of fingerprints. Edward Henry, the British Inspector-General, did not invent the solution. He asked Presidency College for a strong mathematics student and assigned the problem to the officers who arrived.

Qazi Azizul Haque created the mathematical core. He built a formula that sorted every set of ten fingerprints into one of 1,024 distinct categories, arranged as a 32 by 32 grid of pigeonholes. The system rested on the primary division between whorls and loops or arches, with further numerical values assigned according to which fingers carried which patterns. By 1897 thousands of print sets were already filed under this method. A search that previously took about an hour under the old anthropometric system could now be completed in roughly five minutes. Without Haque’s formula there was no practical way to retrieve a matching record from a large collection.

Hem Chandra Bose supplied the technical methods that made the system operational. He developed the further subclassifications that refined the primary sorting, created ways of handling single-digit impressions rather than full sets, and later produced a telegraphic code so fingerprint data could be sent between police stations. His work turned a mathematical filing system into something police forces could actually use day to day. Remove either contribution and the method collapses.

Henry claimed the opposite. He said the classification scheme had come to him in a sudden flash during a train journey and that he had scribbled the idea on his shirt cuff. In 1900 a British committee asked him whether the system was his own invention. He answered yes. He published the monograph Classification and Uses of Fingerprints under his name alone, with no acknowledgement of Haque’s formula or Bose’s methods. The system then spread internationally under the name Henry Classification System.

Henry was rewarded for the claim. He received the Companion of the Star of India, was later knighted, awarded the King’s Police Medal, created a baronet, and rose to become Commissioner of the Metropolitan Police. The system that carried only his name helped secure those honours and his advancement.

Only in the 1920s, when the Government of India reviewed the matter for official recognition of the two officers, did the administrative record state that Haque “actually himself devised the method of classification which is in universal use.” Both men later received titles and payments. None of Henry’s awards were withdrawn and the system kept his name.

If a supervisor today took a subordinate’s formula and technical methods, published them as his own invention, and accepted sole credit, titles and a namesake system, it would be called plagiarism. That is what the record shows happened here. Haque created the mathematics. Bose made the system usable. Henry took the credit and the rewards.
