text:
He has never blinked. Never slept. Never asked for a raise, a break, or a Friday off.

And somewhere tonight, a grown man will walk up to him, look him in the eye, and quietly change his mind about breaking the law.

Hit play, mute it, and watch only the eyes. Then come back. I'm about to explain why this is one of the most underrated security technologies ever built, and why it has nothing to do with electronics.

Thread-length warning: this is long. It is also the most useful thing you will read today about attention, trust, deterrence, and why your brain is easier to hack than any server on earth.

Let's go.

SECURITY IS NOT ABOUT STOPPING CRIMES. IT'S ABOUT CHANGING A DECISION.

Every lock can be picked. Every wall can be climbed. Every alarm can be cut. Security professionals know this, and they say it out loud in rooms the public never sees: nothing is impenetrable. The real job is to make the attempt look like a bad deal.

Criminology has been circling this idea since 1764, when Cesare Beccaria published On Crimes and Punishments. His argument was radical for the time: the certainty of getting caught deters people far more than the severity of the punishment. Modern research keeps landing in the same place. A thief does not run a spreadsheet of prison terms. He runs one question, in about two seconds: will I be seen?

Not "will I be caught." Not "what is the sentence." Will I be seen.

That is the whole game. And the cheapest way to answer that question in the negative for the person standing at your gate is to put something there that looks back at him.

THE OLDEST SECURITY SYSTEM IN HUMAN HISTORY HAS NO BATTERY.

Long before cameras, before sensors, before the word "cybersecurity" existed, humans figured out that a convincing figure with a face does a job that no fence can do.

Scarecrows. Gargoyles on cathedral roofs. Stone guardian lions outside temples across East Asia. Carved watchers at the entrances of tombs. Painted eyes on the bows of ships, so the vessel could "see" its way and watch for danger.

The most extreme example sits in Shaanxi province: the Terracotta Army, roughly 2,200 years old, thousands of life-size soldiers built to guard an emperor in the afterlife. Researchers have long noted that the faces vary from figure to figure. Nobody ordered a factory run of identical soldiers. Someone understood that a crowd of copies looks fake, while a crowd of individuals looks like an army.

Hold that thought. We'll come back to it, because it explains why the figure you just saw is so unsettling.

YOUR BRAIN IS RUNNING A FACE DETECTOR YOU CAN'T SWITCH OFF.

Newborns, within hours of arriving in the world, will turn their heads to follow a face-like pattern more than a scrambled one. Researchers in the 1970s and 1990s showed it, and the finding has been argued over, refined, and reproduced in various forms ever since. The point survives every argument: humans arrive with a prior. Faces matter. Look for them.

This is why you see a face in a power outlet. A face in a car's grille. A face in the clouds. The phenomenon has a name, pareidolia, and it is not a glitch. It is a survival feature that fires early and fires wide, because the cost of missing a real face (a predator, a rival, a parent) was always higher than the cost of seeing a fake one.

Read that again. Your brain is built to over-detect faces.

Now think about what that means for anyone who builds a face on purpose.

THE EYES ARE THE EXPLOIT.

Of all the primates ever studied for this trait, humans stand nearly alone in having a visible white around the iris. The sclera. A 2001 study by Kobayashi and Kohshima compared eye anatomy across primate species and found that humans have by far the most conspicuous eye whites. Most primates hide where they are looking. We broadcast it.

One leading explanation is the cooperative eye hypothesis: we evolved to show our gaze direction because, as a social species, it helped more than it hurt. Where I look tells you what I intend. That made cooperation faster. It also made us extraordinarily sensitive to being watched.

Which is the vulnerability.

Because if your species evolved a gigantic neural investment in tracking other people's gaze, then anything that imitates a gaze gets the investment for free. Two dots on a flat surface can trigger the reaction. A glossy sphere with depth and a highlight on it can trigger it hard.

THE COFFEE EXPERIMENT THAT SHOULD HAVE BEEN FRONT-PAGE NEWS.

In 2006, researchers at Newcastle University ran one of the cleanest and funniest studies in behavioral science. A university staff kitchen operated an honesty box for tea and coffee. A price list hung above it. Each week, the researchers changed the image at the top of the price list. One week, flowers. The next week, a pair of eyes. Then flowers again. Then eyes.

Same room. Same people. Same prices. Same honesty box.

On the weeks with the eyes, people paid for their drinks at nearly three times the rate. The eyes were a photograph. They were not connected to anything. Nobody believed they were being filmed. And behavior moved anyway.

Follow-up work on "watching eyes" has been mixed in the details, as good science always is: some effects shrink, some depend on context, some do not replicate cleanly. But the broad pattern has appeared often enough in field settings that city councils, retailers, and bike-theft prevention campaigns have all borrowed it.

Now take that result and ask a dangerous question: if a printed photograph of eyes can change a person's behavior, what does a three-dimensional face do, wearing a uniform, with eyes that catch the light?

THE FIRST HUNDRED MILLISECONDS.

In 2006, Willis and Todorov showed that people form judgments about a stranger's face, including trustworthiness and competence, after seeing it for about a tenth of a second. More time barely changed those first impressions. It only made people more confident in them.

A tenth of a second is faster than conscious thought. It is shorter than a blink. In that window, the brain has already decided: is that a person, is that person looking at me, and is that person dangerous?

The consequence is brutal and beautiful. A realistic enough figure does not need to survive inspection. It only needs to survive a tenth of a second. After that, doubt arrives, but the behavior has already been nudged. The hesitation has already happened. The thief has already slowed down.

Hesitation is the product. Everything else is packaging.

WHY THE LAST 5 PERCENT OF REALISM COSTS 95 PERCENT OF THE EFFORT.

In 1970, the roboticist Masahiro Mori described what he called the uncanny valley. As a figure becomes more humanlike, our affinity for it rises, until it gets close to human but not quite there. Then affinity collapses into unease. Corpses, mannequins, prosthetic hands, wax faces. The closer to alive, the more the small errors scream.

Here is what most people miss about where the errors hide: they hide in the eyes.

Skin can be forgiven. Skin has pores and sheen and veins and a thousand tolerances. Hair can be forgiven. Even a stiff posture can be forgiven, because people really do stand like statues when they are tired. But eyes are held to a ruthless standard. We scan them first. We scan them longest. And a dead eye, flat, painted, shiny in the wrong way, is the single fastest way to make a human face feel wrong.

So the people who truly master this craft learn one thing before anything else: the eye is not an accessory. The eye is the product. Everything else on the face is a frame for it.

Depth is the secret. A real eye is not a painted disc. It is a wet, curved, layered object: a transparent dome over a colored iris over a dark pupil, with light bending through it. Fake eyes that look fake are flat. Fake eyes that fool people have an illusion of looking through something.

That is the difference between a toy and a threat.

THE CHEAT CODE NOBODY TALKS ABOUT: CLEAR MATERIAL OVER COLOR.

Here is a principle that applies to eyes, jewelry, aquariums, car paint, and screens. If you place a transparent layer above a colored layer, the brain reads depth. The light enters, scatters, and exits at a slightly different angle than it entered. The result looks wet. Looks alive. Looks real.

Ocular prosthetics have run on versions of this idea for centuries. Artificial eyes in the sixteenth century were being made of enameled gold and silver. By the nineteenth century, German glassblowers around Lauscha had made glass eyes into a serious industry, a craft so precise that families guarded their methods across generations. Today, resin, acrylic, and silicone have taken over because they allow the same depth with more control and more durability.

The punchline is almost philosophical. The most realistic part of an artificial face is built from the most transparent material available. Realism is made of nothing. You are looking through it.

A SHORT HISTORY OF MAKING PEOPLE OUT OF WAX.

Marie Tussaud learned wax modeling in Paris, under a physician and modeler named Philippe Curtius, in the years leading up to the French Revolution. When the Revolution arrived, she was reportedly made to produce death masks of people who had just lost their heads. She later carried the craft to Britain, and her exhibition settled in London in 1835. It is still operating nearly two centuries later.

Think about what that business model actually is. People pay money, stand in a queue, and walk into a room filled with silent, motionless, human-shaped objects. And they love it. The reaction is always the same: a pause, a laugh, and then a long look to check whether it is real.

That long look is the entire industry.

Wax, silicone, resin: the materials change. The product does not. You are selling a few seconds of doubt in the nervous system of another human being.

THE ECONOMICS ARE ABSURD.

Let us do the math in the most honest way possible, without pretending to precise numbers.

A human night guard has a salary, which is monthly. Insurance, which is yearly. Sick days, which are unpredictable. Fatigue, which is nightly. A phone, which is a distraction. A bed or a chair, which is an invitation. A bad mood, which is a variable.

A realistic figure has a single cost, paid once. It does not get tired. It does not call in sick. It does not get bribed. It does not fall asleep at 3 a.m. It does not get bored, and it does not scroll.

Is it a better guard? No. A human can respond. A human can call for help. A human can tackle a thief.

But here is the uncomfortable part: for the specific job of making someone decide not to try, the figure is often just as effective, at a tiny fraction of the cost. Because deterrence happens before the action. And before the action, nobody knows whether the guard can respond. They only know whether they feel watched.

Security people have a brutal phrase for this: perceived risk beats actual risk.

THE FAKE CAMERA PARADOX.

Dummy cameras are an enormous and quietly embarrassing market. Plastic housings with a blinking red light and nothing inside. They cost a few dollars. They are sold by the thousand. Security experts will roll their eyes at them, and then admit, privately, that some of them work.

Why? Because the criminal has no way to verify what is inside. Opening the casing takes time. Time is risk. Risk changes decisions.

The same logic applies to the sticker on the window that says an alarm company protects the house. The same logic applies to the "beware of dog" sign on a fence with no dog behind it. The same logic applies to the marked police car parked outside a shop, empty, at the end of a street.

All of these work by planting a belief. And a belief is cheaper than any sensor ever manufactured.

Now put a face on the belief. Give it a uniform. Give it a posture. Give it eyes that follow you.

You have gone from "something might be watching" to "someone is watching."

That is a different animal.

THE GAZE CONE.

Humans are better at detecting that someone is looking directly at them than at detecting precisely where an averted gaze is pointed. Experiments on this go back decades: we hold a surprisingly wide "cone of direct gaze" in which we feel watched even when the eyes are slightly off. In other words, our detector is tuned to over-report. Better to feel stared at by mistake than to miss a real stare.

This is the exact mismatch an artificial face exploits. It does not have to track you. It does not have to be aimed precisely. It only has to sit within the cone. The brain does the rest, filling in the intent, the attention, the threat.

A figure with eyes set slightly wide, glossy, with a believable highlight, positioned at human eye height, does not look at you. You look at it, and you feel looked at.

Read that twice. That's how every great hook works too. We'll get there.

WHY THIS WORKS EVEN WHEN EVERYONE KNOWS IT'S FAKE.

The most surprising thing about deterrence illusions is that they do not require anyone to be fooled. A person can know, intellectually, that the figure is not alive, and still feel a flicker of caution as they approach.

Psychologists have a framework for this. Fast, automatic processing makes the first call. Slow, deliberate reasoning arrives later and corrects it. But the correction is not a delete. The initial impression leaves a residue. A trace of unease that lingers while you reason your way past it.

That residue is not a bug in the design. That residue is the entire design.

You do not need to convince the thief that the guard is real. You only need him to spend four extra seconds checking.

Four seconds is a long time at a gate at night.

THE SCARIEST VERSION OF THIS HAS NOTHING TO DO WITH THIEVES.

Everything above is about security. But the same machinery drives the biggest industries on the planet.

Advertising has understood it for a century: faces sell. Packaging puts eyes on cereal boxes and makes them look slightly downward, toward children, at their eye level. Interface designers know that a face on a screen increases attention and trust. Chatbots, virtual assistants, and avatars are now built with human features specifically because a face lowers resistance.

Every platform you use is a variation on the same trick: find the wiring that evolution built for survival, and pull the lever.

The figure in this video is the honest version. It is physical, visible, and has one job. It does not hide what it is doing, and it does not follow you home.

Much of the digital world cannot say the same.

THE REVERSE QUESTION: WHAT ARE YOU DETERRED BY, WITHOUT KNOWING IT?

Here is the part I would like you to actually sit with.

If a pair of glass eyes can change what a stranger does in the dark, then what else is quietly steering you?

The notification badge you cannot ignore. The "3 people are viewing this" label on a booking page. The countdown timer that costs nothing to produce. The empty chair across a conference table. The unread message with a typing indicator. The profile photo of someone who just liked your post.

You are the guard's target audience in a hundred small ways every day. The hack that works on the thief is the same hack that works on you, and almost nobody notices, because the best version of a trick is the one that feels like your own idea.

WHAT CREATORS CAN STEAL FROM A GUARD WHO DOES NOTHING.

I write about attention. So let's convert this into something you can use on your next post, your next video, your next pitch.

LESSON ONE: Lead with the eyes. In any piece of content, there is one element that the viewer's brain checks first, and if it fails, the rest is invisible. Your first line is the eye. If it looks dead, nothing else gets seen. Spend 80 percent of your effort on the first sentence.

LESSON TWO: Depth beats decoration. A flat claim reads as fake. A claim with a layer of detail over it reads as real. Do not say "huge growth." Say the number, the date, the thing that was different before. A transparent layer of specifics over a colored claim creates depth.
LESSON THREE: Survive the first hundred milliseconds. Readers decide almost instantly. After that, they are not reading. They are confirming. Build the first line to pass the glance test, and build the second line to reward them for staying.

LESSON FOUR: A belief is cheaper than a proof. You do not have to prove every point. You have to make it feel observed, checked, and true. But be careful: this is also the line between persuasion and manipulation. Use the power in the direction of honesty, because the audience that catches you faking it does not come back.
LESSON FIVE: Individual faces beat copies. The Terracotta Army worked because no two faces were alike. Your content works when it has a face too: a specific voice, a specific opinion, a specific scar. The internet is drowning in identical soldiers.

WHAT THE FIGURE DOES THAT YOU CAN'T.
It holds still.

In an economy of constant motion, constant refreshing, constant output, there is real power in a thing that simply stands there and refuses to blink. We have convinced ourselves that attention is won by doing more. But the oldest guard in history wins attention by doing nothing, convincingly.
Think about the last time silence in a room changed the decision. The last time a pause in negotiation made someone cave. The last time a stare at a bar made a loud group go quiet.

Stillness is a signal. Stillness says: I have time. Stillness says: I am sure. Stillness says: you are the one who is hurrying.
THE DARK SIDE.

A responsible version of this post has to include the uncomfortable part.

The same craft that produces a convincing guard also produces a convincing fake of anything. A convincing fake face in a video call. A convincing fake voice on a phone. A convincing fake person behind a convincing fake account. Realism is a neutral technology. It does not care who wields it.

We are moving fast into a world where the cost of faking a human presence is falling toward zero. Faces, voices, motions, even eyes. And the same evolutionary wiring that makes a wax guard work will make a synthetic scammer work. Nothing in your gut is calibrated for that.

The unnerving implication: the skills we are losing are verification skills. The old human habit of checking, of waiting, of asking one more question before you trust. A guard figure can only fool you for four seconds. A well-built synthetic person can fool you for four months.

So the best use of what you just learned is not to build better illusions. It is to catch them.

HOW TO CATCH A FAKE FACE, ANY FACE.

Here are the checks that experts run, and that you can borrow.

Look for the blink pattern. Humans blink irregularly, with clusters and pauses. Perfect rhythm, or none at all, is a tell.

Look for the light in the eyes. In a real eye, the highlight moves as the head moves, and the reflection matches the room. A static, identical highlight at every angle is a tell.

Look for the micro-movements. Living faces are never completely still. Tiny tremors, tiny twitches, tiny asymmetries. Perfect symmetry is not beauty. It is a warning.

Look for the edges. Where the hairline meets the forehead, where the lip meets the skin, where the ear meets the jaw. Real transitions are messy. Fake ones are clean.

Look for context. The most powerful check of all: ask whether this person should be here, saying this, right now. Faces fool you. Situations are harder to fake.

THE QUESTION BEHIND THE QUESTION.

Strip away the craft, the history, the psychology, the economics.

What is this thing, really?

It is an answer to the oldest question in the world of risk: how do I make someone else decide to leave me alone?

For most of history, the answer was force. Walls. Weapons. Armies. Moats full of things that eat you.

Then somebody noticed that you do not need the force. You only need the belief in the force, delivered through the one channel the brain trusts above all others. A face.

And the face does not even have to be good. It has to be good enough for four seconds.

WHAT I'D LIKE YOU TO DO NOW.

Go back to the video.

Watch it again, with a single instruction: do not look at the whole figure. Look at the eyes. Notice the exact moment, if there is one, where your own brain does something. A flinch. A pause. A half-smile. A tiny recoil. A thought you did not choose.

That moment is the thing I have been writing about for twenty sections.

That is your own gaze detector, firing, even though you know the thing in front of you is not a person. That is the guard doing the job. Not on a thief. On you.

If you caught it, you now understand something about your own mind that most people go their entire lives without noticing.

If you did not catch it, watch it again.

THE ONE-LINERS.

For people who scrolled straight to the bottom. Screenshot these.

The cheapest guard is the one the thief believes in.

Security is a story told to a nervous system.

Nothing is impenetrable. Everything is negotiable.

The eye is not part of the face. The face is a frame for the eye.

Realism is mostly transparency over color.

Deterrence happens before the action, so it is won before the fight.

A tenth of a second decides what a lifetime of reasoning will defend.

You do not have to fool anyone. You have to slow them down.

Perceived risk beats actual risk. Every time. In every field.

A fake is not defeated by being exposed. It is defeated by being checked.

Stillness is a signal. Use it.

The Terracotta Army worked because no two faces were the same.

Your first line is your eye. Make it alive.

The best trick is the one that feels like your own idea.

An audience that catches you faking it does not come back.

Hesitation is the product. Everything else is packaging.

The scariest guard is the one that never explains why it's there.

You are the audience for a hundred small illusions per day. Notice three.

Four seconds is a long time at a gate at night.

Attention is not earned by doing more. Sometimes it is earned by refusing to blink.

The guard does not need to be brave. He needs to be believed.

A locked door says "try harder." A watching face says "think again."

If it can make you slow down in the dark, it has already done more than most alarms.

IF YOU STAYED THIS FAR, YOU'RE THE RARE ONE.

Most people never reach the bottom of anything. They glance, they react, they leave. You read twenty-two sections about a figure that does not move, which means your attention is not a commodity. It is a decision, and you made it on purpose.

So here is the deal.

Tell me the exact second you felt it. The flinch, the pause, the half-laugh, the tiny voice that said "is that real?" Put the timestamp in the replies. I read them all, and I will pin the best one.

Repost this if you know someone who builds things people look at: designers, filmmakers, founders, writers, security people, anyone who has ever had three seconds to earn a stranger's trust.

And follow if you want more posts that take one strange object and pull a whole system out of it.

Next time you walk past a doorway, a storefront, a parked car, a poster, a portrait, or a pair of eyes that are not attached to anyone, check your own pulse.

Something there was built to be believed.

Question is: by whom, and for what?

P.S. The strangest part of all of this is how old it is. Every few years someone announces a new frontier in security, a new sensor, a new algorithm, a new dashboard. And every few years the oldest answer in the book quietly keeps working: put a face where a face is expected, and let the human brain finish the job. The technology changes. The audience does not. That is the real moat, and it has always been us. Build for the brain, and the brain will finish the job for you in the dark, each time.

Rachel Clayton: “india’s government is facing fresh questions about press freedom after dozens of journalists were detained while covering youth-led protests. reporters in the capital of new delhi fear the crackdown is part of a wider effort to control what indians see and hear. thousands came to protest, but it was those who came to report. that became the story. the committee to protect journalists says at least 43 reporters were detained while covering this month’s rallies, the vast majority in new delhi. shoaib daniyal has worked for the online newspaper scroll for over a decade.”

Shoaib Daniyal: “there was a checkpoint right outside my house. i spoke to a cop, i asked him about the protest. he became suspicious, he became angry, he said i’m going to detain you. he detained me.”

Rachel Clayton: “shoaib filmed his detention.”

Shoaib Daniyal: “why have you detained me?”

Officer: “you are wasting your time as well as mine.”

Shoaib Daniyal: “for what? what did i do?”

Rachel Clayton: “he says officers offered to release him if he wiped his phone. delete it, the officer tells him. no, he says.”

Shoaib Daniyal: “he didn’t know what to do with me, so he kind of drove me around for almost an hour and a half. eventually, i think they kind of tired themselves out and they did let me go. like, literally anyone could be just picked up and put on the bus. there seems to be no method to segregate people who may genuinely be coming in the way of police work to people who were simply there to report.”

Rachel Clayton: “police are allowed to detain anyone without a warrant under the country’s preventive detention laws, but officers must have a reasonable suspicion the person is going to commit a crime. delhi police claim they could not distinguish between traditional media and protesters filming on their phone. the latest round of demonstrations erupted over india’s election commission. protesters accused commissioner gyanesh kumar of removing millions of names from voter rolls to benefit the ruling bjp government. it comes three months after mass demonstrations forced out india’s education minister, which took everyone, including the government, by surprise.”

Former NDTV journalist: “and i think this was the response of a wounded regime, that they now wanted to hit back. they wanted to stamp out the protests using extraordinary force. and i think silencing or trying to intimidate the media in these new ways is part of that response.”

Rachel Clayton: “where do you see things pointing? he worked for ndtv for 30 years. the network won multiple awards for being india’s most trusted news brand. he resigned in 2022 when businessman gautam adani took over. the billionaire had a close relationship with the prime minister, and journalists raised concerns about editorial independence.”

Former NDTV journalist: “we’ve seen this growing pattern of the gradual takeover of media companies by corporates that are seen as close to the regime. and you also have seen separately media companies on their own flipping. so when that takeover news came, it was kind of a sign that the sort of clock had started ticking. we call them the godi media, meaning lapdog media. what is this dangerous anti-democratic ecosystem that’s being built in this country? entire swaths of particularly tv media have been brought to heel, have turned into propagandists for the government.”

Rachel Clayton: “since narendra modi took power in 2014, the majority of india’s most popular networks have been bought by corporate businesses, politicians, or people with close ties to the government. social media had begun breaking that control. ramit verma creates and publishes political satire for a large online following. he was also detained, covering recent protests. india’s government has tightened its grip on internet freedom and regularly orders social media companies to remove posts and even whole accounts.”

Ramit Verma: “it happened so much that i don’t even remember the last post that got taken down, but it’s become the norm in india right now. it’s become the norm for your posts to get taken down at any point without any explanation.”

Rachel Clayton: “this year’s wave of protests has posed one of the biggest challenges yet to prime minister narendra modi, and the detention of journalists shows the government is not afraid to use authoritarian tactics to stop the media holding those in power to account.”

Former NDTV journalist: “i wouldn’t be surprised if we’ll see a repeat of it. i think there is a kind of marked escalation now that has happened and i don’t quite know if they’re going to roll it back.”

Rachel Clayton: “a worrying sign of things to come. rachel clayton, abc news, new delhi.”

text:
Statement : The removal of BitChat from the India App Store is unconstitutional. Section 69A permits the blocking of unlawful information, not of a messenger for working during internet shutdowns.

New Delhi, 3 October 2026

An Apple App Review notice published today by Jack Dorsey on X records that BitChat has been removed from the India App Store "per demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology", issued under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, on the ground that the application "includes content that is illegal in India". The notice adds that BitChat's TestFlight builds are no longer available for testing in India. It does not identify the content said to be illegal or the ground under Section 69A invoked. The blocking order has not been published. The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns the order and calls for its immediate publication and withdrawal.

BitChat relays end-to-end encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh. It has no servers and hosts no content of its own. What travels through it is the private speech of its users, so the claim that the application "includes" illegal content is incoherent. The State's actual objection stands recorded in the notices the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre issued on 23 July 2026 to GitHub, Google and Apple against BitChat, Briar and Bridgefy which stated that such applications work even during internet shutdowns and hamper lawful interception, attribution and traceability. Those notices, issued under Section 79(3)(b) were reportedly withdrawn after public disclosure. The same end has now been pursued through Section 69A. The objection is to capability of an application, not to content it transmits. A citizen's ability to speak to another citizen while the State has switched the internet off is not a ground of restriction under Section 69A or Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Section 69A survived constitutional scrutiny in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) because of its safeguards which included the need for a reasoned, recorded order, committee review, and a hearing to the originator under Rule 8 of the Blocking Rules, 2009, which the Delhi High Court enforced in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). Further, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published and adopt the least restrictive measure. However, it appears in this instance, each safeguard has been evaded. A secret order blocking an entire application, rather than any identified unlawful information, is the most restrictive and disproprotionate measure available. Further, the confidentiality claimed under Rule 16 cannot defeat the right to challenge an order, and the constitutionality of this blocking regime is itself pending consideration before the Supreme Court.

While removal from the App Store does not delete BitChat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates, leaving existing users on unpatched versions, and it ends security testing in India through TestFlight. During the Jantar Mantar protests, when mobile internet was suspended and jammers were deployed, Bluetooth mesh messaging was a channel of last resort through which young people coordinated their safety. To our knowledge, Apple has removed BitChat on a government's demand in only one other country. This is in China, in April this year.

Our demands

1. MeitY must publish the blocking order, the ground invoked and the record of the committee's proceedings, and serve the developers with a copy and an opportunity of hearing.

2. The direction must be withdrawn. Any specific unlawful use must be met with targeted proceedings under due process, not the removal of a communications tool for everyone.

3. Apple must disclose the demand in its transparency reporting and notify its users in India, and must state whether parallel directions have been received in respect of other app stores.

4. The secrecy of the blocking regime must end. The Blocking Rules, 2009 should be amended to require publication of orders and notice to originators, without awaiting the outcome of the pending constitutional challenge.

The Internet Freedom Foundation will file applications under the Right to Information Act seeking a copy of the order, and stands ready to assist the developers and affected users in India.

I have my twitter back. 

It took me 6 days, a cyber police complaint and a legal notice to twitter to recover my account. 

If you got a DM from me last week asking you to vote for me for a podcast, that was not me. Please don't click it & If you already did, please change your password ASAP.

Here's what happened:

→I received a late night DM from a friend to vote on a podcast which redirected me to a a login page that looked right, and I typed in my password (classic)

→The attacker logged in and changed my 2FA within minutes & I was locked out of my account. (I still don't understand how my email and phone number were changed. Neither my email nor my phone was compromised.)

→Then he used account to DM followers a fake "vote for me" link. Each person who clicks becomes the next account sending it. That is how these spread.

What didn't work:

→ I filed X's hacked account form within the hour. Less than two hours later, the reply came: X could not verify me as the account owner. Their suggestion was to create a new account. Once 2FA is changed, the automated system treats the attacker as the real owner.

→ So I went to the Grievance Officer. Under the IT Rules, 2021, X must appoint a Resident Grievance Officer in India. He has no email address. X does not accept legal notices by email. 

The only options are a web form or post to their physical office.

Here's what worked:

→First, a cyber complaint on https://t.co/Uzds8BObDW (or call 1930).

→Second, a legal notice to the Grievance Officer. Under the IT Rules, impersonation complaints must be acted on within 24 hours.

→Third, the same notice sent by registered post, and to every X email address I could find.

The notice put X on record. It set out the ticket number, the phishing link, and the cyber complaint number. It showed proof of ownership: the registered email, the phone number, and the Premium subscription paid from my card. It ended with a clear ask and a deadline.

Six days after the hack, I was back in.

If this happens to you:
• Act within hours
• File X's hacked account form from your registered email and be persistent (this is important)

• Notice to the Grievance Officer via the https://t.co/YkDfcMQwzE form and by post

text:
MeitY's advisory to Meta directs the suppression of protest reporting on Instagram and Facebook. It must be withdrawn.

19 Oct 2026

On 10 October 2026, the Cyber Laws Division of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued an advisory to Meta Platforms bearing File No. 6(2)/2026-Cyberlaws. It was not published on the MEITY website and first HT and then PTI reported it on 18 October. Any such advisory is not a legal order and MEITY is not legally empowered to issue them on the basis of any statutory provision. This advisory followed, by two days, an advisory of 8 October to all social media intermediaries calling for "enhanced diligence" over content on "ongoing public events", asking platforms to "label or add context" to misleading content and to "give priority to complaints from authorised Government agencies".  IFF called for the withdrawal of that advisory on 9 October. The Meta advisory was issued on the day the Delhi Police detained protesters and journalists at the demonstrations called over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

The advisory states that content relating to "public-order and law and order situations" is being "prominently displayed and recommended" on Meta's platforms and, "when presented without adequate context or disproportionately amplified", "may contribute to public confusion, apprehension and disturbance of public order and social tranquillity". It singles out "unverified or misleading claims regarding the imposition of emergency, restrictions, police action or other official measures". Further, Meta is advised to review its "recommendation and content ranking mechanisms", to ensure its systems "do not result in disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives", and to furnish "information or assistance" to law enforcement, "with immediate effect". PTI reports that the Ministry acted on inputs from "agencies" that Meta's platforms were not promoting all "narratives" equally.

This advisory matches restrictions on META platforms related to protest content and reporting in the same timline. On 10 October, the Instagram account of Molitics India was withheld in India. On 11 October, a Mathrubhumi English reel showing a woman clinging to a pole as police officers attempted to detain her was restricted citing, "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement", and a video report by Observer Post Hindi was restricted on Facebook by what Meta called an "automated system" acting under the IT Rules, 2021. On 12 October, the Instagram account of journalist Shubhangi Das Gupta was restricted in India for alleged non-compliance with "local IT Rules". On 13 October, the account of Journo Mirror (about five lakh followers) was withheld. The account of Fridays For Future India has since been withheld without any stated reason. Meta's notices to these users do not disclose what is unlawful about the content. 

As per notices shared by us by those who have been censored by META, they take two forms: 

1. "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", and, 

2. "through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements under India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules". 

Neither names the issuing agency, the order, the provision of law or offence the content is said to disclose, or the URL complained of. We know due to litigation that the first notice related to a Sahyog order issued by a Law Enforcement Agency (LEA), while the second one is without any legal order. At the same time, several users received no communication at all. Instagram used the same "automated system" notice against Anjali Priya, Varnika Dhawan and Sachin Gupta after the July protests, and against cartoonist Satish Acharya, who lost nine cartoons and then his account between February and September 2026. 

In April 2026, The Hindu reported that Meta automatically restricts government and police flagged content in India at scale, and seeks a separate government direction before restoring content later found to be legally unsupported. IFF objected to Meta on 4 May 2026. IFF condemns the advisory of 10 October and the restrictions imposed in its wake. An executive communication that instructs a platform to suppress "unverified" claims about "police action" and to correct a "limited set of narratives", issued on the day of a police crackdown and kept from the public, is a censorship directive in all but name.  It makes the State the editor of what Indians may see of a protest against the State. IFF calls upon MeitY to withdraw it and upon Meta to disclose what it has done under it.

Our demands

1. MeitY must withdraw the advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026 forthwith and publish them.

2. MeitY must abandon proposed Rule 3(4) and restrict content only by reasoned, published orders under Section 69A or notices compliant with Rule 3(1)(d).

3. Meta must disclose every takedown, account restriction and act of downranking carried out under the advisories, and its compliance report to the Ministry.

4. Meta must restore the accounts and posts of journalists, outlets and creators restricted since 8 October 2026 unless it holds a valid legal order, and must furnish that order to the person affected.

5. Meta must suspend the automated restriction of content in India and disclose on what inputs its "automated system" acts.

Any person whose account or content has been withheld in India since 8 October 2026 may write to IFF at legal@internetfreedom.in. IFF is providing assistance pro bono.

text:
Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Connaught Place ahead of today's protest. We are tracing the suspension order.

New Delhi, 2 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services in and around Connaught Place, New Delhi, this morning. At 9:40 am, Jio subscribers in the area received a message stating: "As per government instructions Internet services have been stopped in your area till further notice." The shutdown took effect before a protest called for 11 am at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner, had even begun. 

Delhi Police has refused permission for the gathering, prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force across New Delhi district, and entry and exit at eleven metro stations have been closed. On Gandhi Jayanti, the answer to a call for protest in the capital has been to switch off the internet for everyone who lives, works, trades and reports in its centre. We call for the immediate restoration of services. 

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public does not know who directed this shutdown, on what grounds, over what area, or until when. IFF is attempting to trace the order and will make it public as soon as we obtain a copy.

In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Supreme Court held that speech and trade over the internet are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution, and that every suspension order must be published, reasoned, proportionate and limited in time. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, only the Union or State Home Secretary may issue such an order, for reasons recorded in writing. The order must be published and must specify the area, the services and a fixed duration and it may be passed only where no other reasonable means would serve. A shutdown announced to subscribers as lasting "till further notice", imposed before a single person had assembled, cannot be squared with these safeguards. It follows repeated suspensions around Jantar Mantar in July 2026. Switching off the network is becoming a routine response to protest in the national capital. IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. 

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore mobile internet services in Connaught Place and all affected parts of Central Delhi.

2. Publish the suspension order forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.

3. Disclose the issuing authority, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation.

4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and make its findings public.

10. MATRIX Encrypted Platform – 2024

Foreign VPN Use in Crimes in India (2020–2025)

Here are 10 news reports from 2020–2025 detailing cases where foreign VPNs (or non-compliant international VPN services) were used to commit or facilitate crimes against children (CSAM/pornography), women (sextortion/cyberstalking), terrorism/national security threats, or other serious offenses (ransomware/fraud/drug trafficking) in India. Each includes a brief summary, crime type, and primary source link.

1. Sharp Rise in CSAM Demand via VPNs (2020)

Crime: Cyber fraud/ransomware-like theft → Times of India

Sir, the pattern is undeniable:

- Foreign VPNs openly defy Indian law.
- They enable child exploitation, pornography, violence against women, radicalization, drug trafficking and terrorist activity.

Requested Immediate Possible Actions for Consideration:

1. Publish a National Registry of Compliant VPNs
Direct CERT-In and MeitY to publish and maintain a public registry of VPN providers that have demonstrated compliance with the 28 April 2022 CERT-In Directions issued under the Information Technology Act, 2000.
Requirement: Five-year data logging, real-time incident reporting, and appointment of an Indian-resident nodal officer.
Purpose: Establish transparency and a verifiable compliance benchmark for enforcement.

2. Delist and Prohibit Operation of Non-Compliant Foreign VPNs
Instruct Apple, Google, and all Indian ISPs to immediately delist and block all non-compliant foreign VPNs, including NordVPN, ProtonVPN, ExpressVPN, Surfshark, and Mullvad, that have refused to adhere to the 2022 CERT-In Directions.
Action: To be taken under the blocking powers of the Information Technology Act and its associated Intermediary Guidelines.
Purpose: Prevent evasion of Indian jurisdiction and close routes for offenders hiding behind virtual foreign IPs.

3. Block Associated Payment Channels
Direct the Reserve Bank of India and all licensed payment aggregators and card networks such as PayU, Razorpay, Visa, and Mastercard to suspend or block subscription transactions to banned or non-compliant VPN providers.
Purpose: Cut off domestic funding and revenue flows sustaining illegal VPN operations.

4. Mandate Exclusive Use of CERT-In Certified VPNs
Require, through regulatory notification, that only VPNs, whether Indian or foreign, that obtain CERT-In certification be permitted to operate in India.
All VPNs advertising Indian IP services must maintain logging infrastructure within Indian jurisdiction and comply with lawful requests from enforcement agencies.
Purpose: Ensure traceability and lawful accountability of all VPN activity associated with Indian IP addresses.

5. Criminalise Intentional Use for Concealment During Offences
Propose suitable amendments or notifications under the Information Technology Act and India’s relevant penal codes to criminalise the intentional use of banned or non-compliant VPNs for concealing identity during the commission of cognisable offences involving child sexual abuse material, terrorism, radicalisation, or financial fraud.
Purpose: Target deliberate misuse while preserving lawful privacy.

6. Strengthen Traceability and Cooperation
Mandate that every VPN provider operating in India:
(a) Designate a resident nodal officer;
(b) Retain subscriber and metadata for five years; and
(c) Respond to law enforcement requests within seventy-two hours, as required by the CERT-In Directions of 2022.
Purpose: Guarantee swift investigatory access while preserving due process.

7. Establish a National Honeypot and Canarytoken Programme
Authorise CERT-In and the National Cybercrime Threat Analytics Unit to deploy a nationwide honeypot and Canarytoken framework, as validated in peer-reviewed research, to trace VPN-enabled crimes involving child sexual abuse material, sextortion, ransomware, and terror financing.
Ensure judicial oversight, privacy protection, and certified chain of custody for admissibility of digital evidence.
Purpose: Build indigenous technical capability to unmask offenders using VPN anonymity.

8. Strengthen International Coordination and FATF Alignment
Direct NIA, CBI, and MHA’s Cyber Coordination Centre to:
(a) Formalise fast-track cooperation with FBI, Europol, and Interpol under Mutual Legal Assistance Treaties; and
(b) Report VPN-linked money-laundering or terror-financing incidents to the Financial Action Task Force in conformity with its Comprehensive Update on Terrorist Financing Risks dated 8 July 2025.
Purpose: Integrate India’s enforcement with global counter-terror and cybercrime frameworks.

9. Institute Annual CERT-In Audit and Enforcement Schedule
Require annual audits of VPN providers’ compliance and publish audit summaries for public accountability.
Providers failing to comply beyond sixty days after notice should face permanent blocking and notifications to RBI, DoT, and MeitY for coordinated enforcement.
Purpose: Ensure continuous oversight and eliminate recurring non-compliance.

10. Issue a Public Advisory and Compliance Deadline
Issue a national advisory within thirty days, notifying all VPN providers of a sixty-day compliance window.
After the deadline, non-compliant entities should face delisting, domain blocking, and payment interdiction without exception.
Purpose: Provide procedural fairness before enforcement action begins.

India must not remain a playground for foreign tools that shield sexual predators, criminals and terrorists. The Ministry of Home Affairs has already acted strictly—forcing Apple and Google to delist 6+ non-compliant VPNs in January 2025. It is time to complete the job.

Vande Mataram

text:
Statement: Instagram censors a cartoon about censorship. IFF will challenge it.
A cartoon on comedy, copyright and the IT Rules has been withheld in India by an automated system that cites no order and gives no reasons.

On 27 October 2026, Instagram withheld in India a cartoon by Aadvik (@aaaaadvik ) who first published on 29 September 2026 as a collaborative post on the accounts of IFF, Aadvik and stand-up comedian Pulkit Mani. It shows a panicked man at a console in the image and style of the Prime Minister with red buttons marked "Censor", "Copyright" and "IT Rules", while a comic performs on a screen above him. Its caption reads, "Quick, check if comedy counts as a violation of copyright or a matter of national security." The post asked who decides what gets taken down, and on what grounds.

Instagram has now answered this literally by taking it down after close to a month. Its notice says access was restricted "through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements" under the IT Rules, 2021. It names no order, authority, provision or ground. There was no prior notice and no chance to respond. The same cartoon remains available on IFF's X account. The post also carried an update on Pulkit Mani v. Meta Platforms Inc. & Ors., his Delhi High Court suit over fraudulent copyright strikes on his Instagram page, in which IFF appears for him pro bono. Meta, a defendant in that suit, has now hidden a post about it from Indian users in which it is the principal defendant.

In 1945, George Orwell wrote a preface to Animal Farm, a book four publishers had turned down. He noted, "the sinister fact about literary censorship in England," he observed, "is that it is largely voluntary." Unpopular ideas, he argued, could be silenced without any official ban, by institutions that guess what power wants and act first. The preface itself stayed unpublished until 1972 and in Nineteen Eighty-Four he gave this habit a machine, namely, the memory hole, a slot at the Ministry of Truth into which inconvenient records vanished, unexplained and beyond appeal. Today, the Ministry of Electronics and IT acts as this Ministry of Truth that covers up its gross incompetence in securing our cyber security by building an architecture of digital censorship that is implemented by technology platforms. It is under these IT Rules, 2021 that Instagram's "automated system" exists as a memory hole. It has swallowed a cartoon whose whole joke is a man reaching for the censor button without asking what comedy is. The absurdity Aadvik drew has now been actually demonstrated in stark reality.

This machine did not build itself and in April 2026, The Hindu reported that Meta automatically restricts content flagged by government and police in India, and wants a fresh government direction before restoring anything later found lawful. MeitY's unpublished advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026 pressed platforms, and Meta by name, for "enhanced diligence". The same notice has been served on cartoonist Satish Acharya, who lost nine cartoons and then his account, on journalists covering the October protests, and days ago on comedian Kajol Srinivasan. The Union Government applies the pressure and Meta has chosen to answer it with a system that censors first and explains nothing.

IFF will soon challenge Meta's automated restriction system in an appropriate legal proceeding. A joke is not a threat to the nation, and we will not let Meta’s algorithms decide otherwise.

Our demands
1) Meta must restore the post in India, and tell IFF, Aadvik and Pulkit Mani which order, authority and provision it relied on, if any.
2) Meta must suspend the automated restriction of content in India and disclose the inputs on which its "automated system" acts.
3) MeitY must state whether any direction, Sahyog Portal intimation or advisory concerned this cartoon, and withdraw and publish its advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026.
4) The Union Government must restrict content only by reasoned, published orders under Section 69A or by intimations that comply with Rule 3(1)(d), and never by leaning on platforms.

Speak up
A memory hole works only as long as people accept it in silence. If you are a cartoonist, comic, creator or journalist whose post or account has been withheld with this notice, write to us at legal@internetfreedom.in with screenshots of every notice and we will try our best to provide you help pro-bono. Over the past 72 hours we have assisted close to 56 social media users, some of whom had their accounts restored. We are in this together!

Constitution Day here!🫡

Preamble comes with most tricky questions😮

Learn everything about Preamble in this SINGLE post

• Intro
• History
• Keywords
• Objectives
• Court Cases
• Other details for #UPSC 

Save this to notes🔖

& you are done for this topic!

________________________
Before you read ahead, note:

I am coming up with a special Constitution Class November 26 2023 onwards

Here, you will learn tips & tricks on how to learn Constitution Articles

Join my Telegram from link in my bio to avail access to this

Back to post👇🏼
__________

1. Introduction

Preamble explains philosophy & objectives of Constitution

As a living document, 

it defines the core values & principles ‘for the nation’

Importantly, it gives an idea on:

• Source
• Nature of state
• Objectives of Constitution
• Date of adoption: 26/11/1949

You will remember this with mnemonic: SNOD

Also, Nov 26 is celebrated as Constitution day due to this date!

2. History

• Liberty, Equality, Fraternity (LEF): 
Taken from French constitution

• Ideals of Preamble:
Laid down in Objective Resolution proposed by Pt. Nehru

• It is not enforceable in the courts

3. Keywords & Objectives

This is the section from where you see most Q

Note these carefully one by one

• We, the people of India

Rests ultimate sovereignty in hands of people of India

None but people determine independent authority of the state

• Sovereign

India has independent authority

Henceforth, Indian legislature will make its own laws

(Note: Not absolute laws, tho!)

• Socialist

An indicator of faith in mixed economy

It reflects direction as to achieve socialist ends via democratic means

(Note: Added by 42nd Amendment Act in 1976)

• Secular

Equal protection, respect & state support

To whom? All religions!

(Note: Added by 42nd Amendment Act in 1976)

• Democratic

Indian Constitution sets up an authority

This authority is expressed in elections as will of people

What for? A democratic process!

• Republic

Simple words: Head of state to be elected by People

In Indian sense, President is elected ‘indirectly’ by people of India

Further, Constitution has a main objective:

To promote harmony throughout the nation

How’s this ensured? Objectives!

How’re objectives achieved?

Through some factors as stated below

• Justice

A necessary factor to maintain societal order

Both, Fundamental Rights & DPSP enable justice

There are three elements to this:

(You can remember it with SEP)

a) Social Justice

No cast, creed, gender, religion based discrimination

b) Economic Justice

• No discrimination on economic basis
• Equal pay for equal work

c) Political Justice

No discrimination to participate in political opportunities

(Can be seen in right to vote or no educational barrier to fight election)

• Equality

Everyone is equal before law i.e.

No special privileges to any section of society

• Liberty

All people have freedom to:

Choose way of life, have politics views & behavior in society

(Note: Liberty to do anything but within limits of the law)

• Fraternity

Brotherhood feeling among all people

It aims to promote dignity & unity in the nation

Okay CSEWhy, I get all of these BUT

Why are these objectives important?

These are important to provide a way of life!

All of these are interconnected. How?

• Liberty & equality can’t exist without each other

• Liberty & equality can’t be natural without fraternity

• With no equality, liberty will put few supreme over many

• Individual initiative will be killed in equality w/o liberty

(all are linked)

4. Court Cases

Status of preamble has led to many cases

Find these summarized below👇🏼

• Berubari Union Case 1960

A case of Indo-Pak agreement to exchange enclaves reached SC

Referred u/A 143 by President,

8 judges sat down to discuss the matter. Outcome?

Preamble is key to open the mind of the makers’ but it can not be considered as part of the constitution

Therefore, it is not enforceable in a court of law! 😮

• Kesavananda Bharati Case 1973

13 judges sat down to hear a write petition

About preamble, these were observations:

a) Preamble is a part of the constitution

b) Not supreme power or source of any restriction but plays an important role in interpretation of statutes & provisions

Conclusion: 
It is part of introductory part of constitution

• Union of Govt. v/s LIC of India 1995

SC: “Preamble is integral part but not enforceable in court of justice in India”

5. Other details

• Preamble can be amended u/A 368 (sans basic structure)

• 42nd Amendment Act 1976

a) Added Socialist, Secular, & Integrity

b) ‘Unity of Nation’ changed to ‘Unity & Integrity of Nation’

• On 26/11/1949, following articles came into force:

a) Citizenship: Articles 5-9
b) Oath of President: Article 60
c) Election Commission: Article 324

..along with: 367, 379 & 394

(rest all on 26/01/1950)

Mains Question:

2016 UPSC Mains Question:

Discuss each objective attached to the word ‘Republic’ in the ‘Preamble’. Are they defendable in present circumstances?

Write answer to this Question and email to whycse[at]gmail[dot]com for evaluation! :)

text:
INDIA TO IDENTIFY ALL TELEGRAM, WHATSAPP AND SIGNAL USERS WITH "SIM BINDING"

India is set to enforce "SIM binding" for major messaging apps from around January 1, 2027.

What is the ruling

The Department of Telecommunications (@DoT_India) directed platforms including WhatsApp (@WhatsApp), Telegram (@telegram), Signal (@signalapp), Snapchat (@Snapchat), others in 2025 to keep accounts continuously linked to the specific active SIM used for registration.

If that SIM is removed, deactivated or swapped, the app should stop working on the device until the correct SIM is present and verified.

iOS has long blocked apps from directly reading SIM status or hardware identifiers. Apple (@Apple) released a software patch in September that lets apps detect when an iPhone lacks a SIM card, making compliance possible for messaging apps. Apple has not issued a detailed public statement on its reasoning. Earlier queries to the company went unanswered.

What it means for online privacy

The rule does not break end-to-end encryption. It does, however, strengthen the permanent link between a messaging account, a telecom-issued phone number, and the owner's identity.

The Department of Telecommunications runs platforms such as the Digital Intelligence Platform (DIP) and Sanchar Saathi (TAFCOP). These aggregate connection data across operators so authorities can see how SIMs are linked to an individual's verified identity.

Claimed motivation

The government want to identify everyone online.

The government says the rule closes a loophole that lets accounts keep working after the SIM is removed or the number is used from abroad. This has been exploited for phishing, impersonation, "digital arrest" scams and other fraud. Officials cite large cyber-fraud losses and argue that tying accounts to KYC-verified telecom identities improves traceability, similar to existing SIM/device binding already used in banking and UPI (@NPCI_NPCI) apps.

Experts' opinion

Fraudsters routinely obtain SIMs with weak or fake KYC, use them briefly, and discard them. Binding does little against that or against malware, phishing kits and session hijacking.

Industry groups such as IAMAI (@IAMAIForum) have argued the rule mainly creates friction for ordinary users while leaving core attack vectors largely intact,

India's record on using online deanonymising tools

India has a documented pattern of using legal, technical, and policing tools to restrict online speech, target critics, and limit communications during protests—actions frequently criticized by human-rights organisations as disproportionate or politically selective. The new SIM-binding and related telecom identification rules increase the technical capacity to track identity-linked communications, raising the practical risk of similar misuse even if the stated purpose is "fraud prevention".

Reporters Without Borders (@RSF_inter) ranked India 157th out of 180 in its 2026 World Press Freedom Index. RSF and others cite violence against journalists, heavy concentration of media ownership linked to figures close to the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (@BJP4India), and the increasing use of criminal laws against reporters and critics.

Section 69A of the IT Act is the main blocking tool. In 2026, orders have targeted satirical cartoons critical of the prime minister, fact-checker posts, media outlets such as The Wire (@thewire_in), and accounts posting political criticism or mockery.

In October 2026, during demonstrations in Delhi linked to voter-roll revisions and the "Cockroach Janta Party" movement, which criticised the Election Commission (@ECISVEEP), authorities imposed mobile-internet blackouts, conducted mass detentions (including opposition leaders such as Rahul Gandhi and journalists, and reportedly monitored messaging groups.

What can concerned Indians do?

Practical steps for Indians concerned about online privacy are limited by mandatory SIM ID checks, biometric rules, and SIM-binding requirements, but they can still meaningfully reduce exposure.

True anonymity is difficult in India because almost all consumer SIMs are tied to verified identity through ID checks and increasingly biometric checks.

👉 Prefer Signal for sensitive conversations. It has stronger default end-to-end encryption and collects less metadata than WhatsApp. Both will still be subject to SIM-binding, but Signal's design is more privacy-oriented.

👉 Use a reputable no-logs VPN (Mullvad (@mullvadnet), Proton VPN (@ProtonVPN) for sensitive browsing or public Wi-Fi. Note that CERT-In (@IndianCERT) logging rules led most privacy-focused providers to remove physical servers from India; many now offer virtual Indian IPs hosted abroad.

👉 Enable disappearing messages, turn off read receipts where possible, and verify safety numbers for important contacts.

👉 Restrict who can see your phone number, profile photo, last seen, and "about" status (set to "My contacts" or "Nobody").

👉 Avoid using the same number for banking, government services, and casual or sensitive chats if you can manage a second number within the legal 9-SIM limit.
